articles.title: "Mandatory user verification" on DEV is a scam. Here's how to spot it in 30 seconds.
articles.description: If you got tagged by "Support Bot" on DEV, don't click.  It took one look at the profile:   The name...
articles.body_html:
If you got tagged by "Support Bot" on DEV, don't click.

It took one look at the profile:

  • The name isn't "Support". It's Cyrillic letters dressed as Latin ones: "Suрроrt Воt".
  • The account was created on Nov 4: 0 posts, 41 comments when I looked.
  • It tags 10 people per comment, in alphabetical order, ten at a time. Nobody at DEV works through the alphabet by hand.
  • The username has already changed: my notification says salemsalem123, the profile now says supportbot123.

No real platform verifies you through a stranger's comment, and none needs your card for it.

Clicked but typed nothing? Close the tab, clear that site's data, check your downloads.

Authorized something or typed a password? Revoke the app and change the password now.

Entered your card? Call your bank.

Then flag the account: profile, then "Flag" or "Mark as Spam".

Check the profile before the link. It takes ten seconds, and it would have stopped this one cold.

articles.title: Svelte 5 Isn't Pure Compiler Magic: How Runes, Fine-Grained Signals, and Direct DOM Mutations Actually Work Under the Hood
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute deep dive into Svelte 5 internals. Learn why Svelte shifted from compile-time dirty checking to runtime signals, how the Push-Pull reactive dependency graph works, how the compiler compiles templates into direct DOM operations without a Virtual DOM, and when to use $state.raw for maximum performance.
articles.body_html:
When Svelte first captured the web development community, it arrived with a bold manifesto:

"Virtual DOM is pure overhead. Svelte runs at build time, converting your components into tiny, highly efficient vanilla JavaScript that surgically updates the DOM."

For five years, developers celebrated Svelte's compile-time reactivity. You did not need useState, dependency arrays, or reconciliation engines. You simply wrote ordinary JavaScript:

<script>
  let count = 0;

  function increment() {
    count += 1;
  }
</script>

<button on:click={increment}>
  Clicks: {count}
</button>

Under the hood, Svelte 3 and 4 parsed your script, spotted the assignment operator (count += 1), and injected a hidden compiler helper called $$invalidate:

function increment() {
  $$invalidate(0, count += 1);
}

Whenever $$invalidate fired, Svelte flagged a bitmask dirty array on the component instance. On the next microtask, it walked through a switch statement in the generated update function and mutated the exact DOM node.

It felt like sorcery. But as applications scaled, that pure compile-time illusion began showing deep architectural cracks.

Reactivity only worked inside .svelte single file components. If you moved business logic into a standalone JavaScript file, the compiler could no longer rewrite your variable assignments. You had to abandon normal variables and reach for custom Svelte stores with manual subscriptions, readable contracts, and awkward boilerplate. Furthermore, tracking deep object mutations required reassigning the root object (user.profile.age = 30; user = user;), causing the entire component to re-evaluate its dirty checks.

With Svelte 5, the core team made an audacious architectural pivot. They walked away from pure compile-time assignment rewriting and adopted Runes: explicit primitives powered by a fine-grained, push-pull runtime signal graph.

Many developers were startled. Was Svelte turning into Solid or Vue? Did Svelte abandon its core philosophy?

The reality is far more fascinating. Svelte 5 did not surrender its compiler advantage; it elevated it. By combining static template hoisting with runtime signals, Svelte 5 achieves fine-grained reactivity without the clunky stores of Svelte 4, and without the Virtual DOM overhead of React.

Here is the mechanical breakdown of how Svelte 5 actually executes beneath your keyboard.

1. The Architectural Shift: Svelte 4 vs Svelte 5

To understand why Runes exist, you must inspect the assembly line of Svelte 4.

In Svelte 4, the compiler treated the entire .svelte component as the atomic boundary of reactivity. When you modified a variable, the component did not know which specific DOM node depended on which specific sub-property. The compiler only knew that something inside the component was dirty.

Here is what Svelte 4 generated for a simple counter:

// Svelte 4 Compiler Output (Conceptual)
function p(ctx, [dirty]) {
  // If bit 0 in the dirty bitmask is set:
  if (dirty & /*count*/ 1) {
    set_data(t1, /*count*/ ctx[0]);
  }
}

This model came with three severe limitations:

  1. The Component Boundary Trap: If you wanted reactive state shared across five components or held in a TypeScript utility file, you could not use let count = 0. You had to import writable(0) from svelte/store, wrap updates in count.update(n => n + 1), and use the special auto-subscription syntax ($count) inside templates.
  2. Coarse-Grained Dirty Checking: Every state change marked the entire component dirty. Even if only one text node changed, Svelte had to execute the component's p() update function, checking every active bitmask condition.
  3. Array and Object Mutation Pitfalls: Methods like array.push(item) did not trigger reactivity because no assignment operator existed for the AST parser to rewrite. Developers had to write array = [...array, item] purely to appease the compiler.

Svelte 5 solves this by moving reactivity from compile-time AST variable instrumentation to universal runtime signal nodes.

Instead of rewriting count += 1, Svelte 5 provides primitives called Runes ($state, $derived, $effect). These functions do not belong to a preprocessor; they are parsed into universal signal nodes that work identically inside .svelte files and universal .svelte.js or .svelte.ts modules.

2. Under the Hood of Runes: The Push-Pull Signal Graph

When you declare state in Svelte 5:

let count = $state(0);
let double = $derived(count * 2);

You are not creating a simple number. You are registering nodes inside a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of reactive dependencies.

A signal graph consists of three primary node types:

  • Source Nodes ($state): Hold raw values. When written to, they notify their dependents.
  • Computation Nodes ($derived): Depend on one or more sources or other computations. They recalculate only when their upstream dependencies change.
  • Consumer Nodes ($effect): Side effects and DOM update bindings that subscribe to sources or derivations and run when their inputs change.

Most naive signal implementations use an eager push mechanism: when a source changes, it immediately pushes the new value down every branch of the tree. This approach frequently causes the Diamond Problem, where a node that depends on two derived values is evaluated twice in intermediate, inconsistent states (a glitch).

Svelte 5 avoids this completely using a Push-Pull (or Mark-and-Sweep) algorithm.

The Push Phase (Marking Dirty)

When you write count++, Svelte does not immediately recalculate double or update the DOM. Instead, it enters a synchronous push phase:

  1. The $state(count) source node marks itself as dirty.
  2. It walks down its dependency links to $derived(double).
  3. It does not recompute double; it simply marks double with a status flag: DIRTY.
  4. It continues downstream to any active $effect connected to double, scheduling the effect into the microtask execution queue.

No application logic runs during the push phase. Only lightweight status flags are toggled.

The Pull Phase (Lazy Evaluation)

When the browser reaches the scheduled microtask or when application code reads double:

  1. The consumer pulls the value from $derived(double).
  2. The derivation checks its flag. If it is DIRTY, it checks its upstream dependency (count).
  3. It computes the new value (count * 2), caches the result, and clears its DIRTY flag.
  4. If double is read ten times without count changing, it returns the cached value in $O(1)$ time with zero recalculation.

This separation guarantees glitch-free execution. If two different derivations depend on the same counter and feed into a single effect, the effect runs exactly once, reading both values after all dirty marks have resolved.

3. The Compiler Pipeline: Turning Templates into Vanilla JS

If Svelte 5 uses runtime signals, what role does the compiler play?

This is where Svelte 5 departs dramatically from signal-based frameworks like SolidJS. SolidJS creates individual reactive wrappers around almost every element. Svelte 5 uses its compiler to perform Static Template Hoisting and Surgical Dynamic Attachment.

Consider this Svelte 5 component:

<script>
  let count = $state(0);
  let user = $state("Ada");
</script>

<div class="card">
  <h1>Welcome, {user}!</h1>
  <p>Static description text that never changes.</p>
  <button onclick={() => count++}>
    Clicks: {count}
  </button>
</div>

When you pass this file through svelte/compiler, the compilation passes through four distinct phases:

Phase 1: Parsing and AST Construction

The compiler parses the file into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), separating the <script> block, CSS styles, and HTML elements into structured nodes.

Phase 2: Static Analysis

The compiler walks the template tree and identifies which parts of the markup are completely static. In our example:

  • <div class="card"> is static.
  • <h1>Welcome, </h1> has static tags with one dynamic text slot ({user}).
  • <p>Static description...</p> is completely static.
  • <button> has a dynamic event listener and one dynamic text slot ({count}).

Phase 3: Template Hoisting ($.template)

Instead of compiling each HTML element into separate JavaScript document creation calls (document.createElement('div')), the compiler stringifies the entire invariant HTML structure into a single static string template:

// Compiled output (conceptual representation)
const root_template = $.template(
  `<div class="card">
    <h1>Welcome, <!>!</h1>
    <p>Static description text that never changes.</p>
    <button>Clicks: <!></button>
  </div>`
);

Notice the <!> comment markers. These serve as hydration anchors and insertion slots for dynamic expressions.

At application initialization, the browser calls document.createElement('template') and parses this HTML string natively in C++ through the browser engine. When a component instance mounts, Svelte clones this entire pre-parsed subtree using root_template(), which executes a single, hyper-fast document.importNode() clone.

Phase 4: Targeted Effect Subscriptions ($.render_effect)

Next, the compiler generates code that traverses directly to the dynamic slots without inspecting the static nodes:

export default function Component($$anchor) {
  let count = $.source(0);
  let user = $.source("Ada");

  const fragment = root_template();
  const div = $.first_child(fragment);
  const h1 = $.first_child(div);
  const user_text_slot = $.child(h1, 1);
  const button = $.sibling($.sibling(h1, 2), 2);
  const count_text_slot = $.child(button, 1);

  // Bind event listener
  button.__click = () => $.set(count, $.get(count) + 1);

  // Subscribe dynamic text nodes to signals
  $.render_effect(() => {
    $.set_text(user_text_slot, $.get(user));
  });

  $.render_effect(() => {
    $.set_text(count_text_slot, $.get(count));
  });

  $.append($$anchor, fragment);
}

Look closely at what happened.

The static <p> tag is never stored in a variable, never inspected by a reconciliation algorithm, and never diffed.

When count changes, only the second $.render_effect wakes up. It reads the new value and executes count_text_slot.data = new_value. The parent component function does not re-run. No intermediate JavaScript objects are allocated. The update is a direct, surgical $O(1)$ memory write.

4. Virtual DOM vs Direct Signal Mutation: The Real Memory Cost

To truly appreciate this architecture, compare it to how React handles the same counter button.

In React, state belongs to the component fiber. When you call setCount(count + 1):

  1. React marks the entire component fiber dirty.
  2. The scheduler re-executes the component function from top to bottom.
  3. Every JSX expression executes, instantiating fresh Virtual DOM JavaScript objects for the <div>, the <h1>, the <p>, and the <button>.
  4. The reconciler diffs the newly created virtual tree against the previous virtual tree.
  5. It discovers that the text node inside <button> changed, creates a DOM patch, and writes to the real DOM.
  6. The entire abandoned virtual tree is discarded and awaits garbage collection.

In simple apps, this process happens in a fraction of a millisecond. But in large dashboards, data tables, or heavy data-visualization tools with thousands of nodes, allocating and diffing virtual trees generates non-trivial CPU work and persistent garbage collection pressure.

In Svelte 5:

  • The component function runs once at mount.
  • When count increments, zero virtual DOM nodes are instantiated.
  • Zero diffing algorithms run.
  • The signal triggers its subscriber directly: node.data = count.

Because Svelte does not need a runtime reconciliation engine, the core client runtime weighs only a few kilobytes.

5. Deep Proxy Reactivity vs $state.raw: Performance at Scale

One of the most powerful features of Svelte 5 is deep object reactivity. In Svelte 4, mutating an array or nested object required reassignment gymnastics. In Svelte 5, $state wraps objects in JavaScript Proxy instances:

let settings = $state({
  theme: "dark",
  user: {
    notifications: {
      email: true
    }
  }
});

// Works seamlessly:
settings.user.notifications.email = false;

When you pass an object or array to $state(), Svelte recursively intercepts read and write operations. When you mutate settings.user.notifications.email, the proxy trap catches the write, identifies the exact signal node associated with that property path, and notifies only the effects reading that specific leaf property.

However, deep proxying comes with an engineering tradeoff: memory overhead.

If you fetch a dataset of 50,000 GeoJSON points, financial transactions, or WebGL coordinate buffers and wrap it in $state(), Svelte will recursively proxy every single object and array index in that collection. That proxy creation consumes significant CPU time and multiplies heap memory consumption.

To solve this, Svelte 5 introduced $state.raw.

When to Use $state.raw

$state.raw creates a shallow signal that does not proxy its contents:

// Creates a shallow signal with ZERO proxy wrapping
let bigData = $state.raw(largePayloadFromApi);

// This will NOT trigger reactivity:
bigData[0].selected = true;

// Reassigning the root reference DOES trigger reactivity:
bigData = bigData.map(item => 
  item.id === targetId ? { ...item, selected: true } : item
);

Use $state.raw whenever:

  1. You are managing large, immutable datasets (tables with thousands of rows, API responses).
  2. You are integrating third-party libraries that hold their own complex class instances (Three.js meshes, Leaflet map objects, Monaco editor instances). Wrapping these in Proxies can break internal identity checks (this === target).
  3. You only care about updates when replacing the entire reference.

By distinguishing between $state for interactive UI state and $state.raw for large data buffers, you can maintain optimal frame rates and minimal heap footprints.

6. Production Pitfalls: The $effect Trap

Because $effect resembles React's useEffect, developers transitioning to Svelte 5 often carry over dangerous habits.

The most common antipattern is using $effect for state synchronization:

// ❌ ANTIPATTERN: Redundant state synchronization
let count = $state(0);
let double = $state(0);

$effect(() => {
  double = count * 2;
});

Why is this dangerous?

  1. It forces two distinct render cycles. First, count changes and renders. Next, the effect runs, mutates double, and triggers a second render pass.
  2. It breaks the signal graph's push-pull guarantees, creating potential infinite loops if dependencies are not strictly isolated.

The idiomatic Svelte 5 approach is to use $derived:

// ✅ IDIOMATIC: Synchronous, lazy derivation
let count = $state(0);
let double = $derived(count * 2);

$derived calculates its value synchronously during the pull phase, costs zero effect scheduler overhead, and guarantees that downstream consumers always see consistent data on the very first render pass.

Reserve $effect strictly for true external side effects:

  • Manual DOM manipulation (canvas painting, focusing an input).
  • Setting up external event listeners or WebSocket subscriptions.
  • Logging analytics or saving state to localStorage.

7. Universal Reactivity in .svelte.js Modules

Perhaps the most transformative benefit of Svelte 5 is that reactivity is no longer trapped inside component markup.

In Svelte 4, building a reusable reactive state machine across files required custom stores:

// Svelte 4: Store boilerplate in cart.js
import { writable, derived } from 'svelte/store';

export const items = writable([]);
export const total = derived(items, $items => 
  $items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0)
);

export function addItem(item) {
  items.update(list => [...list, item]);
}

In Svelte 5, you create a standard .svelte.js or .svelte.ts file and write ordinary JavaScript classes or factory functions using Runes:

// Svelte 5: cart.svelte.ts
export class Cart {
  items = $state<Item[]>([]);
  total = $derived(this.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0));

  add(item: Item) {
    this.items.push(item);
  }

  remove(id: string) {
    this.items = this.items.filter(i => i.id !== id);
  }
}

export const cart = new Cart();

Any component that imports cart can read cart.total or call cart.add(item) directly. Because Cart uses native signals, components automatically subscribe to only the properties they access. If a component only reads cart.total, it will not re-evaluate when an individual item's thumbnail updates.

Reactivity is now a native language feature of your application architecture rather than a special syntax reserved for template files.

The Mental Shift

The transition from Svelte 4 to Svelte 5 is not an admission that compilers failed. It is the realization that the compiler and the runtime signal graph are strongest when working in harmony.

The compiler excels at static analysis: finding invariant HTML, hoisting templates into pre-parsed DOM clones, and isolating reactive holes at build time.

Runtime signals excel at dynamic dependencies: tracking relationships across module boundaries, managing deep object mutations without reassignment hacks, and executing push-pull updates without dirty bitmask arrays.

By pairing a specialized build-time compiler with a fine-grained signal engine, Svelte 5 delivers what front-end architectures have promised for a decade: the expressive simplicity of vanilla JavaScript variables with the surgical precision of direct DOM updates.

If you have migrated existing production applications to Svelte 5, how has the transition from Svelte 4 stores to Runes shaped your state architecture? Have you encountered cases where $state.raw made a measurable difference in memory consumption? Share your findings and architectural patterns in the comments below.

articles.title: Securing an Angular Firebase AI App with Email/Password Authentication (Part 3: Lightweight Home Screen, Lazy CDK Dialog, and Header Navigation)
articles.description: We now have AuthService for authentication and SignInModalComponent for users to enter their email...
articles.body_html:
We now have AuthService for authentication and SignInModalComponent for users to enter their email and password, and we need a lightweight home screen (HomeComponent) to connect them. When a user is unauthenticated, clicking the Sign In button on the home screen opens the CDK Sign-In modal. The user then enters their email and password to complete authentication and navigate to the /dashboard route.

In addition, HeaderComponent no longer displays only static text. It now renders a Home icon link on the left edge and a conditional Sign-Out button on the right edge.


Caption: The unauthenticated Home screen displaying the left-aligned Home icon in the header, the "Sign In" button in the hero card, and the feature metadata cards.

Architecture & Mental Model

HomeComponent and HeaderComponent share the AuthService.isAuthenticated computed signal to coordinate the UI across three states:

  • Unauthenticated /home: HeaderComponent displays only the left-aligned Home icon link (/home), and HomeComponent renders the Sign In button.
  • Lazy-loaded CDK Dialog (openSignInModal()): Clicking Sign In dynamically imports SignInModalComponent and Dialog (@angular/cdk/dialog) with Promise.all(), keeping the CDK dialog and Signal Forms out of the initial main.js bundle.
  • Authenticated /dashboard and /home: Once signed in, HeaderComponent reveals the right-aligned Sign-Out button. When an authenticated user returns to /home, HomeComponent checks isAuthenticated() and displays the Launch Studio link (/dashboard) instead of the Sign In button. 
flowchart LR
    subgraph Header["HeaderComponent (app-header)"]
        HOME_ICON["HomeIconComponent ([routerLink]='/home')"]
        AUTH_HDR{"isAuthenticated()?"}
        SIGNOUT_BTN["SignOutIconComponent (onSignOut -> /home)"]
        AUTH_HDR -- "true" --> SIGNOUT_BTN
    end

    subgraph Home["HomeComponent (/home)"]
        RESTORE["constructor: ensureAuth().catch(...)"]
        AUTH_HOME{"isAuthenticated()?"}
        SIGNIN_BTN["Button: Sign In (openSignInModal)"]
        LAUNCH_LINK["Link: Launch Studio ([routerLink]='/dashboard')"]
        RESTORE --> AUTH_HOME
        AUTH_HOME -- "false" --> SIGNIN_BTN
        AUTH_HOME -- "true" --> LAUNCH_LINK
    end

    subgraph LazyModal["Deferred Modal Chunk"]
        IMPORT["Promise.all([import(SignInModalComponent), import('@angular/cdk/dialog')])"]
        INJECT["runInInjectionContext(#injector, () => inject(Dialog).open(...))"]
        IMPORT --> INJECT
    end

    SIGNIN_BTN --> IMPORT
    INJECT -- "Auth Success" --> AUTH_HOME
    INJECT -- "Auth Success" --> AUTH_HDR

1. Updating HeaderComponent with Home Navigation and Conditional Sign-Out

In HeaderComponent, we add home navigation and a conditional Sign-Out button:

  • Component imports: Imports HomeIconComponent, RouterLink, and SignOutIconComponent in the imports array.
  • Home link: Displays <app-home-icon /> inside an <a> tag with [routerLink]="homeLink" (APP_LINKS.HOME, or /home) to navigate to the home screen on click.
  • Sign-Out button: Shows the <app-sign-out-icon /> button only when isAuthenticated() is true; clicking it calls onSignOut() to sign out, update isAuthenticated(), and return to /home. 
// src/app/shared/ui/layout/header/header.component.ts
@Component({
  selector: 'app-header',
  imports: [HomeIconComponent, RouterLink, SignOutIconComponent],
})
export class HeaderComponent {
  readonly homeLink = APP_LINKS.HOME;
  readonly #authService = inject(AuthService);
  readonly #router = inject(Router);
  readonly isAuthenticated = this.#authService.isAuthenticated;

  async onSignOut(): Promise<void> {
    await this.#authService.signOut();
    await this.#router.navigate([APP_LINKS.HOME]);
  }
}

<!-- src/app/shared/ui/layout/header/header.component.html -->
<header>
  <a [routerLink]="homeLink" aria-label="Go to Home Screen">
    <app-home-icon />
  </a>
  <h1>Firebase AI Logic Obscure Fact Speech Generator</h1>
  @if (isAuthenticated()) {
    <button type="button" (click)="onSignOut()" aria-label="Sign out">
      <app-sign-out-icon />
    </button>
  }
</header>

2. Building the Lightweight HomeComponent & Lazy-Loading the CDK Dialog

2.1 Restoring Auth State in the Constructor (ensureAuth().catch(...))

We need to ensure that the Firebase Auth Emulator and Firebase Auth are properly initialized when HomeComponent is constructed. However, a constructor() cannot be async, so we must execute this.#authService.ensureAuth() with a Promise chain instead of async/await.

The .catch() block logs and silently swallows any error without rethrowing it. Because this background task does not require the user's attention, showing an error message here would only cause confusion and unwanted panic.

// src/app/features/home/home.component.ts (Part 1: Fields & Constructor)
@Component({
  selector: 'app-home',
  imports: [RouterLink, ArrowRightIconComponent],
})
export class HomeComponent {
  readonly dashboard = APP_LINKS.DASHBOARD;
  readonly #authService = inject(AuthService);
  readonly isAuthenticated = this.#authService.isAuthenticated;
  readonly #injector = inject(Injector);
  #dialogRef: DialogRef<unknown, SignInModalComponent> | null = null;
  #isOpeningModal = false;

  constructor() {
    this.#authService.ensureAuth().catch((error) => console.error('Failed to restore auth session:', error));
  }

2.2 Lazy-Loading @angular/cdk/dialog & Solving the NG0203 Injection Context Error with runInInjectionContext

When opening the Sign-In modal in openSignInModal(), we keep the initial bundle small while preserving Angular's injection context:

  • Keeping main.js lightweight: Because HomeComponent is eagerly loaded into the main.js bundle, any static import increases its raw size and transfer time.
  • Lazy-loading @angular/cdk/dialog and the NG0203 error: We optimize the bundle by dynamically importing SignInModalComponent and @angular/cdk/dialog in openSignInModal(). However, calling inject(Dialog) after await Promise.all(...) throws an NG0203 error because it runs outside a valid injection context.
  • Restoring the injection context: We solve this by running the dialog logic inside the callback of runInInjectionContext using HomeComponent's Injector (this.#injector).
  • Why runInInjectionContext over a higher-order function: Using runInInjectionContext lets us assign this.#dialogRef = dialogRef directly inside an arrow function, which is cleaner than passing .bind(this) to a higher-order function.

2.3 Preventing Duplicate Modals & Resetting this.#dialogRef on Close (dialogRef.closed.subscribe)

In openSignInModal(), we prevent duplicate Sign-In modals and clean up the dialog reference on close:

  • Guarding against duplicate modals: #isOpeningModal and #dialogRef prevent opening multiple Sign-In modals; when either is truthy, a modal is already opening or open, so the method exits early.
  • Lazy-loading and opening the modal: Otherwise, we dynamically import SignInModalComponent and @angular/cdk/dialog with Promise.all(), inject Dialog to open the modal, and store its reference in this.#dialogRef.
  • Resetting #dialogRef on close: Subscribing to dialogRef.closed resets this.#dialogRef to null when the modal closes, allowing the dialog to be reopened later. 
// src/app/features/home/home.component.ts (Part 2: openSignInModal)
  async openSignInModal(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.#isOpeningModal || this.#dialogRef) {
      return;
    }

    this.#isOpeningModal = true;
    try {
      const [{ SignInModalComponent }, { Dialog }] = await Promise.all([
        import('@/shared/ui/sign-in-modal/sign-in-modal.component'),
        import('@angular/cdk/dialog'),
      ]);
      runInInjectionContext(this.#injector, () => {
        const dialog = inject(Dialog);
        const dialogRef = dialog.open(SignInModalComponent, {
          backdropClass: ['bg-surface-card'],
        });

        this.#dialogRef = dialogRef;
        dialogRef.closed.subscribe(() => (this.#dialogRef = null));
      });
    } finally {
      this.#isOpeningModal = false;
    }
  }
}

2.4 Conditional CTA Rendering in home.component.html

In home.component.html, the isAuthenticated() computed signal determines which button to display—including when a user navigates back to /home by typing /home in the address bar or clicking the Home icon in HeaderComponent:

  • When isAuthenticated() is true: The Home screen renders a Launch Studio link ([routerLink]="dashboard") that routes directly to /dashboard.
  • When isAuthenticated() is false: The Home screen renders a Sign In button ((click)="openSignInModal()") that opens the CDK Sign-In modal. 
<!-- src/app/features/home/home.component.html (CTA excerpt) -->
@if (isAuthenticated()) {
  <a [routerLink]="dashboard">
    <span>Launch Studio</span>
    <app-arrow-right-icon />
  </a>
} @else {
  <button type="button" (click)="openSignInModal()">
    <span>Sign In</span>
  </button>
}


Caption: The authenticated Home screen displaying the Home icon on the left and Sign-Out icon on the right of the header, and the "Launch Studio" button in the hero card.

Takeaways

In Part 3, we completed our authentication flow by connecting HomeComponent, SignInModalComponent, and HeaderComponent:

  • Conditional Actions in HomeComponent: We built a lightweight HomeComponent that conditionally renders the Sign In and Launch Studio buttons based on the isAuthenticated() signal. When isAuthenticated() is false, it displays the Sign In button; when true, it displays Launch Studio.
  • Lazy CDK Sign-In Modal Flow: Clicking Sign In opens the CDK SignInModalComponent where users enter their email and password. When the credentials are valid, the modal navigates the user to the /dashboard route; otherwise, it displays an authentication error message.
  • Resolving NG0203 with runInInjectionContext: Injecting Dialog after await Promise.all(...) in openSignInModal() triggers Angular's NG0203 error because the async continuation runs outside an injection context. We resolve this by executing the dialog logic inside the callback of runInInjectionContext using HomeComponent's Injector.
  • Header Navigation and Sign-Out: HeaderComponent adds home navigation and sign-out functionality. It always displays the Home icon to navigate back to the /home screen when clicked, while the conditional Sign-Out icon allows authenticated users to sign out from Firebase Auth and reset the isAuthenticated() signal to false.

  • Angular CDK Dialog Overview
  • Angular Dependency Injection Context (runInInjectionContext)

articles.title: Nuxt CLI v4 Is Great for AI Coding Agents
articles.description: Have you ever had a dev server running, and then asked your coding agent to test something in that...
articles.body_html:
Have you ever had a dev server running, and then asked your coding agent to test something in that app? It starts its own server on port 3001. Then it restarts that one, and you end up with another on 3002. Pretty soon you've lost track of what's running on which port and what you need to stop...

Nuxt CLI v4 shipped alongside Nuxt 4.6 in early October, and a few of its new features fix that exact problem. The Nuxt team pitched this release as a speed and dev experience update. Nuxt's own numbers put the CLI install at 3.5 MB (down from 13.1 MB) and first paint for nuxt dev at 50 ms (down from 330 ms). However, what I'm really interested in is some of the agentic features.

I tried them on a small Nuxt 4.6.4 todo app. Here's the video if you'd rather watch:

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 22.21+, 24.11+, or 26+. CLI v4 won't run on older versions.
  • A Nuxt project on 4.6 or later. CLI v4 is a dependency of nuxt, so upgrading Nuxt gets you the new CLI. I tested nuxt 4.6.4 with @nuxt/cli 4.0.3.
  • Optional, a coding agent that can run shell commands.

1. Meet the new nuxt dev

Run npm run dev and the first thing you'll notice is the panel pinned to the bottom of your terminal. It shows your Nuxt version, the local URL, a request counter, and a row of single-key shortcuts.


The new nuxt dev panel. Each letter at the bottom is a shortcut.

r restarts the server, o opens it in the browser, i shows info about your setup, and n lists every request with its status and timing. Press p for all your pages and server routes. If you'd rather have plain log output, nuxt dev --no-tui turns the panel off.

2. Check the lock file

When nuxt dev starts, it writes .nuxt/nuxt.lock. When you stop the server, the file goes away. Here's mine:


.nuxt/nuxt.lock has everything an agent needs to find the running server.

The PID, port, and URL tell an agent that a server is already up and where to find it. It doesn't have to probe ports or guess at localhost:3000.

The interactive field records whether the server was started from an interactive terminal. Nuxt uses it to decide what happens when a second nuxt dev shows up. In my testing, a server started from a real terminal wouldn't hand itself over to a non-interactive nuxt dev (the kind an agent runs). The agent gets a message pointing it at --takeover instead. A server that was started non-interactively gets taken over on the same port, so an agent that restarts its own server doesn't leave the old one running.

3. Run nuxt dev a second time

If you run npm run dev again while a server is up, Nuxt stops and asks what you want:


Taking over stops the running server. Start anyway gives you a second one.

Take over stops the running server and starts yours on the same port. That's the --takeover flag. Start anyway runs a second server, which you can also force with NUXT_IGNORE_LOCK=1. Nuxt calls that unsupported.

The CLI already warns an agent about all of this, but I still wanted the rules written down. So I added a steering file at .kiro/steering/nuxt-dev-server.md. If you use a different agent, put the same thing in AGENTS.md.

---
inclusion: always
---

# Nuxt dev server rules

This project uses Nuxt 4.6 with Nuxt CLI v4.

- Never start a second `nuxt dev`. A dev server is usually already running. Check `.nuxt/nuxt.lock` for its URL.
- Never pass `--takeover` or set `NUXT_IGNORE_LOCK=1` unless I ask.
- To test API routes, use `npx nuxt curl <path>` (add `-X`, `-d`, `-i` as needed). It finds the running server without a port.
- To run Nitro tasks, use `npx nuxt task list` and `npx nuxt task run <name> --payload.<key>=<value>`.
- Before using a Nuxt API you are unsure about, run `npx nuxt docs "<query>"` to read the docs for the installed version.

4. Test routes with nuxt curl

If the agent can't start its own server, it still needs a way to test things. That's what nuxt curl is for.

npx nuxt curl /api/todos


No host, no port. nuxt curl reads the lock file.

You pass a path, not a URL. nuxt curl reads the lock file, finds the running server, and pretty-prints the JSON it gets back. It takes the usual curl flags too, so a POST looks like this:

npx nuxt curl /api/todos -X POST -d '{"title":"Added by nuxt curl"}'

Add -i to see the response headers. If no server is running, it tells you to start one with nuxt dev or pass an absolute URL.

5. Run Nitro tasks with nuxt task

The other command I liked is nuxt task, which runs Nitro tasks against the running server. Tasks are still experimental in Nitro, so turn them on in nuxt.config.ts first:

export default defineNuxtConfig({
  nitro: {
    experimental: { tasks: true },
  },
})

My app has a seed task in server/tasks/db/seed.ts that resets the in-memory todos:

export default defineTask({
  meta: {
    name: 'db:seed',
    description: 'Replace the in-memory todos with N seeded todos',
  },
  run({ payload }) {
    const count = Math.min(Math.max(Number(payload?.count) || 5, 1), 100)
    const todos = resetTodos(count)
    return { result: `Seeded ${todos.length} todos` }
  },
})

Then list and run it from the terminal:

npx nuxt task list
npx nuxt task run db:seed


I forgot the run subcommand the first time. The help output got me there.

You can see I typed npx nuxt task db:seed first and got an error. It needs run. Pass a payload with --payload.count=10 and you get 10 todos instead of the default 5.

6. Hand errors to your agent

I really like this the most, because I run into this all the time! In my example my app has a /profile page that's broken on purpose:

<script setup lang="ts">
const user = { name: 'Erik', profile: null as null | { handle: string } }
const handle = user.profile!.handle.toUpperCase()
</script>

Load it and Nuxt shows the new error overlay. You get the error, the exact line in profile.vue, a toggle between source and compiled code, and a call stack with the 9 framework frames hidden by default.


The Copy error menu has an option written for agents.

The new part is the Copy error menu. Copy as Markdown and Copy structured JSON do what they sound like. Copy prompt for an agent wraps the error, source location, Node version, and runtime details in instructions to diagnose the error, trace the root cause, and explain the failure.

I pasted that prompt into Kiro, running Claude Opus 5.5, and let it go. Because of the steering file, it didn't start a server. It ran npx nuxt curl /profile to confirm the 500, changed the non-null assertion to optional chaining and added a v-if so the template skips the missing handle, then ran nuxt curl again to confirm a 200.


Kiro checked its own fix with nuxt curl against my running server.

The whole thing took about 36 seconds and one credit.

Wrap up

I'm really liking this new version of Nuxt CLI! I'd like to see more frameworks do this. Have you had an agent take over your dev server, or start five of them? Let me know in the comments.

Links

  • Nuxt 4.6 release post
  • Nuxt CLI v4.0.0 release notes
  • Nitro tasks docs
  • Kiro steering docs
  • Kiro
  • The video on YouTube

articles.title: How I build products with AI: from a brainstorm to a production release
articles.description: When I start a product, I open ChatGPT before I open a coding agent.  I want to work through the idea...
articles.body_html:
When I start a product, I open ChatGPT before I open a coding agent.

I want to work through the idea before anything starts creating files. Who needs this product? What belongs in the first version? What am I deliberately leaving out? I want to settle those questions while changing my mind still means editing a document.

Then I move between tools: ChatGPT for the requirements, Antigravity for the GitHub backlog, Copilot CLI for implementation, and Claude Code for review. I read the final pull request myself before deciding whether to merge. GitHub Actions carries the work through validation and deployment, with different triggers for previews and production releases.

I also want the same engineering setup when I switch tools or start another product. I use skills for that, and I created dotcraft, my plugin of skills and agents for .NET, Blazor, and MudBlazor. It gives me a reusable starting point instead of another setup to assemble.

My setup:

Work Tool Model or setting
Brainstorming and PRD ChatGPT GPT-6.1 Sol, high reasoning
Initial application logo ChatGPT PRD as context
Everyday work without a model preference GitHub Copilot Copilot Fusion
Epics and child issues Antigravity with GitHub CLI Gemini 3.8 Flash, high reasoning
Epic implementation GitHub Copilot CLI with dotcraft GPT-6.1 Luna (or Copilot Fusion), Max reasoning, YOLO mode
AI review Claude Code app or CLI Claude Opus 5.5
UI work Copilot or Antigravity with the relevant skills A deliberate choice: GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, or Gemini Flash
Repeatable browser checks Playwright Automated user flows and assertions
Final review Me Read the code and check the behavior
Delivery and releases GitHub Actions CI, development previews, and production deployment

The model names will change. What I want to keep is the context: a decision made during the brainstorm needs to survive all the way to the code I merge.

Lately, Fusion is my default

I don't choose a model manually for every request. Lately, I use Copilot Fusion for most work where I don't already have a reason to pick a particular model. I give it the task and let it handle model selection.

Copilot Fusion selected at the Standard tier in my model picker.

UI work is an example of when I do have a preference: I might specifically want GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra. That is when I make the choice myself. For the rest, Fusion has been working very well for me, and I have found it helps keep my token costs down. I haven't measured a fixed saving per task.

I switched to Copilot Fusion recently because I was experimenting with it during the Preview (it was called HydraFusion) but I was not enthusiast about the outcomes.

I keep the model and billing details in my GitHub Copilot guide in the Resources section of my website. The named-model handoffs below describe particular parts of my workflow; Fusion is what I increasingly use between those cases.

The PRD carries my decisions between tools

My ChatGPT conversation ends with a product requirements document, or PRD, in the repository. I use GPT-6.1 Sol with high reasoning to work through the scope before asking for that document.

"Users can export their data" is the sort of requirement I want to question here. Which data? Which format? Does it include archived records? If I leave those decisions open, the implementation agent has to make them for me.

I put the PRD somewhere every tool can read it, such as docs/PRD.md. If I change a requirement, I update the file. A decision that exists only in my ChatGPT conversation is missing context for the next session.

The PRD also gives me a starting point for the initial application logo. I use it in ChatGPT to explain the product and audience, ask for a few directions, and choose one before generating the image. At this stage, I care about whether the logo works in an application header and as a small icon.

Sometimes I also use the logo-generator skill by op7418. That is a separate skill I use alongside dotcraft.

Then I open Antigravity and ask Gemini 3.8 Flash with high reasoning to turn the PRD into epics and child issues through the GitHub CLI. In my experience, this step has been accurate and inexpensive. I still check the backlog before implementation starts.

This is a reusable version of the request:

Read docs/PRD.md and the repository instructions.
Check existing issues and the applicable issue templates,
including account defaults.

Use the GitHub CLI to create epics and child issues.
Each epic needs a product outcome and scope.
Each child issue needs acceptance criteria, dependencies,
and a reference to the relevant PRD section.

Use native parent/sub-issue relationships.
Do not invent requirements or create duplicates.
Report unresolved decisions and return the created issue URLs.

I don't need to create and link every issue by hand. I do need to check that the agent has preserved the scope. A backlog full of clear titles can still describe a different product from the one I intended.

I check all the Epics and Issues anyway and I fix something if I see something that I don't really like so much.\
I like also this approach because if something that AI implement and I don't like it, I can always rework on the single task or epic using the same description and prompt.\
It helps to obtain always the same outcome.

dotcraft is how I keep my setup with me

For my .NET products, I want business logic to live in the application services and component tests to follow the same conventions. Switching from Copilot to Claude Code should not mean explaining those choices again.

That is why I created kasuken/dotcraft. It packages skills I have written, adapted, or curated from other projects, together with agents for implementation, review, and cleanup. I can maintain the shared guidance in one place and reuse it across products.

One shared setup for the .NET products I build. The repository also credits the skills' upstream sources.

For example, blazor-saas-stack describes my default architecture. bunit-testing provides guidance for component tests. dotnet-validate defines the verification expected before a change is called done. I don't want to paste all of those instructions into every implementation prompt.

The agents give the work separate roles: csharp-expert implements .NET changes, code-reviewer reads the result and reports findings, and janitor handles cleanup in small steps.

The implementation agent is instructed to validate its changes and hand them to the reviewer. Those instructions still need to be checked against what happened in the session.

In Copilot CLI, I install the plugin with:

copilot plugin marketplace add kasuken/dotcraft
copilot plugin install dotcraft@dotcraft

dotcraft also documents installation for Claude Code and Codex. Each client needs its own setup; installing a plugin in Copilot does not configure Antigravity. For Antigravity, I make the relevant skills available in a supported skill location.

The product's own instructions take precedence over dotcraft's defaults. I keep project decisions in AGENTS.md and the instruction files the client recognizes, then check that the client has found them. In Copilot CLI, /instructions and /skills list help me inspect the setup. A skill appearing in the list establishes availability; I still check that it is loaded when the task needs it.

I also maintain kasuken/.github for shared issue and pull request templates. The feature request form asks for the problem before the proposed solution. The PR checklist asks for testing evidence and includes a check that the app still works with billing disabled.
Using this approach, I don't need to configure common things in all my repos and I increase the bootstrapping of a new project.

The shared PR template gives me specific questions to ask of a change, including what happens when paid features are disabled.

GitHub supplies these supported defaults when a repository has no local equivalent. They are not copied into a clone, so a local agent may need to fetch them. I ask for that explicitly rather than assume a PR created through gh will contain the checklist.

DayPulse gave me a useful example

For DayPulse, one of my private projects, GPT-6 Sol produced the PRD and I gave it to Antigravity to create the backlog. The Today Screen epic had two child issues.

The first covered the localized date and the empty state when there was no check-in for the user's local day, with an action leading to /checkin. The second covered the completed check-in summary, including optional metrics, activities, notes, and navigation to edit or view the entry.

DayPulse's check-in screen with mood and energy selected. Screenshot from my application.

That local-day requirement is a detail I care about. "Show today's check-in" leaves room for an implementation to use the server's date. Specifying the user's local day gives me something concrete to check in the code and tests. The summary issue also explicitly required disabled metrics to stay hidden.

I handed GPT-6 Luna with Max reasoning the whole epic in one request. I then asked Claude Opus 5.5 to review the implementation across the epic; it reported no findings.

The issue completion notes recorded 253 passing tests after the first child issue and 284 in the final Release validation, with no build warnings or errors. Those are reported validation totals, including existing tests. They are not counts of tests the agent wrote for those two issues.

For me, the useful result was being able to compare the implementation with those specific acceptance criteria. A review with no findings doesn't answer whether I asked for the right product behavior.

I hand Copilot an epic with a clear stopping point

For the explicit-model implementation route described here, I open Copilot CLI with dotcraft installed, select GPT-6 Luna with Max reasoning, and enable YOLO mode. Some single-issue runs have used around 10–15 Copilot credits in my experience; that is a rough observation, not a price to budget against.

My request covers the epic and its child issues, with a separate commit for each issue and one pull request at the end:

Implement the epic at <EPIC_URL> and all its child issues.
Read the repository instructions, PRD, and applicable installed skills.
Work on a dedicated feature branch and respect issue dependencies.

Validate each child issue against its acceptance criteria.
Automate repeatable browser flows with Playwright where applicable.
Report automated coverage and anything that still needs a manual check.
Create a coherent commit for each issue and reference its URL.
Record completion and actual validation results on the issues.

Close the epic only when every child issue is implemented and validated.
Leave blocked work open and explain the blocker.

Create a PR using the applicable template, including an issue-to-commit
mapping, validation results, and remaining limitations.
Do not merge the PR.

One commit per issue lets me inspect the parts of the epic separately. In this workflow, closing the epic means implementation is ready for review; it does not mean the feature has shipped.

YOLO mode removes repeated approval prompts through Copilot's allow-all permissions. It does not make the commands safe. I am choosing to give the agent that permission, and I remain responsible for what it does.

After Copilot opens the PR, I ask Claude Code to review the implementation across the whole epic. I usually keep review fixes in that PR and rerun the affected checks if the code changes. I need validation for the version I am considering merging.

Then I read the final code myself and check the behavior against the requirements. That is where I decide whether to accept the work.

UI work gets a different route through the same process

For UI work, I want to choose the model myself when I have a particular result in mind. That might mean GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra in Copilot. I also use Antigravity with Gemini Flash, which has given me good UI results. I choose the tool and model for that piece of work, then return to Fusion when I have no reason to keep a specific model selected.

For the "general" UI and Design System I love the skill frontend-design because it helps AI to create the correct UI based on the context of the application and not the typical slop AI.

I bring in skills such as mudblazor-design-system, better-layout, and better-typography to make the request more specific. I also check keyboard and focus behavior. A screenshot helps me judge the layout, but I still need to use the form and see what happens in the empty state.

The requirements stay in the repository and the result still gets reviewed. Changing the tool for UI work should not mean losing the acceptance criteria I already settled.

I automate the repeatable browser checks with Playwright

I try to automate as much of the application testing as I can with Playwright. I don't want to click through the same screens manually after every change when a browser test can repeat the steps and check the result for me.

For a flow like DayPulse's check-in, I want the test to start from the empty Today screen, create an entry, verify the summary, edit the entry, and check that the updated values appear. Opening each page successfully isn't enough; the assertions need to cover the behavior in the acceptance criteria. This is the kind of repeatable journey I want automated as the product grows.

In Brainy, the CI workflow already has a separate Playwright end-to-end test job. It runs against the application with a real SQL Server database and is configured to upload traces and screenshots when tests fail. That gives me something to inspect when a browser test breaks, alongside the agent's explanation.

I still review whether the interface makes sense and explore behavior the tests don't cover. My aim is to spend that time on things that need my judgment, while Playwright handles the checks I would otherwise repeat by hand. I also review the tests: they need to fail when the expected behavior breaks.

I finish the backlog, then check the application as a whole

I repeat the implementation and review loop for the remaining epics in the release scope. Before calling that scope complete, I go back through the parent epics and their child issues. I want to see which PR contains the implementation, what was validated, and whether anything is still blocked or deliberately deferred.

An agent closing an epic is useful bookkeeping, but I still reconcile it with the merged code. If a child issue is incomplete, I leave it open. If I decide a feature belongs in a later release, I update the scope rather than close the issue as though it had been implemented.

I can ask an agent to help with that final pass:

Review the epics in the current release scope against the PRD,
their child issues, and the merged pull requests.

For each epic, report the implementation PRs, validation evidence,
and any unmet acceptance criteria. Check the child issues themselves;
do not rely only on the parent's checklist or closed status.

Close remaining issues only when the implementation and validation
support doing so. Leave blocked or deferred work open and explain why.
Report any requirements that are missing from the backlog.

Then I check the application across those epic boundaries, using automated browser tests for the repeatable journeys and manual checks for the remaining gaps. In DayPulse, the empty Today screen, the check-in form, and the completed summary need to work as one flow. Reviewing each screen separately would leave that journey unchecked.

The same applies to UI changes made late in the process: a better layout still needs to preserve navigation, validation, and the behavior described in the issues. I make corrections through the same issue and PR loop, so the fix gets reviewed too.

GitHub Actions gives me a development preview

I don't want deployment to depend on an agent remembering a sequence of terminal commands. I keep the build, test, and deployment steps in GitHub Actions so that the repository describes how the application gets published.

DayPulse is a concrete example. Its workflow runs a Release build and the test suite before the deployment job can start. For pull requests from the same repository, it is configured to publish the Blazor WebAssembly application to an Azure Static Web Apps preview environment. That gives me a development preview associated with the PR, before the change reaches production.

This is where I can check the published application in the browser. DayPulse is also a PWA, so I need to check installation, offline reload, and upgrades against a published build. The local development server alone doesn't cover those behaviors.

After I accept and merge the change, the push to main triggers DayPulse's build, test, and deployment workflow for production. Closing the PR also triggers cleanup of its preview environment. The automation handles the repeated publishing steps; I still check the workflow result and the deployed application.

Production releases have an explicit trigger

My server-hosted SaaS applications use a different production path. For Brainy, LearnStack, MoneyBrain, and Needly, I maintain a shared release workflow in kasuken/.github. Each application calls it from a small workflow in its own repository.

For these applications, merging to main runs CI without automatically deploying to production. I choose when to cut a release; GitHub Actions then handles the deployment. The distinction matters to me because several reviewed epics can belong to one release.

The release instructions let me choose a patch, minor, or major bump. For example, this starts a patch release for Brainy:

gh workflow run release.yml -R kasuken/Brainy -f bump=patch
gh run watch -R kasuken/Brainy

For that new-release path, the workflow resolves the next version, waits for passing CI on the commit being released, and builds a versioned application package. It deploys that package to Azure App Service through the GitHub production environment, using OIDC for Azure authentication.

Database changes are part of that delivery path too. Needly's migrations run before deployment; the other applications in this shared setup apply them on startup. I need to account for that difference when reviewing a release, especially if I might need to restore an earlier application version.

The workflow then checks the readiness endpoint, any configured extra pages, and the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect. On the workflow-dispatched new-release path, it creates the version tag and GitHub release only after deployment and those smoke checks succeed. It uses the matching changelog section for the notes when one exists, or generates notes from the merged PRs.

That is another part of the setup I want to maintain once. An improvement to the shared workflow can serve several products, while the application repositories supply their own project paths and deployment targets.

After deployment, I still have a product to check

A passing readiness check tells me the application responds. I also want evidence that the user flow I intended to release still works. I use automated checks where that behavior is covered and focus my manual review on the remaining gaps. For DayPulse, the Today and check-in journey, including the local-day behavior, remains the reference for what needs checking in the published application.

If I find a problem, it goes back into an issue with reproduction steps and the behavior I expected. I can give that bounded task to an agent, review the correction, and send it through the same delivery process. The backlog remains useful after the initial implementation.

For applications using my shared release workflow, I can redeploy an earlier version tag when I need to roll back. That restores the earlier application code; it does not reverse database migrations. I need to check that the older version still works with the current schema before choosing that route.

This is where the workflow reaches a release: the code has been reviewed, the intended version has been deployed, and I have checked the relevant behavior in the running application. Closing all the epics gets me to that final check; it doesn't replace it.

I like working this way in Omarchy

In Omarchy, I keep the browser full-screen on one workspace and three or four terminals tiled on another. Copilot can be working in one terminal while I inspect tests or Git history in another. Switching workspaces and moving focus with the keyboard lets me keep those layouts in place.

Four-way tiling, shown in the official Omarchy navigation manual. This is the manual's example desktop.

I have tried to reproduce the same behavior on Windows. Getting the tiling, workspace switching, and window focus to feel the way I want has taken more effort there. On Omarchy, I spend less time rearranging the desktop.

The searchable clipboard history is useful when I am carrying an issue URL or prompt between tools. I also like the themes running through the terminal and supported agent clients. I like sitting down at this machine, and that matters when it is where I build my products.

Searching copied text, from the official Omarchy clipboard manual. The example shows how a copied command can be found again.

I still spend attention on the scope, the backlog, and the final review. dotcraft saves me from rebuilding the engineering setup, and GitHub Actions handles the repeated release steps. Neither can decide whether DayPulse should show that metric or whether a feature belongs in the first release. Those decisions are still mine, and I want to see them reflected in the application I publish.

articles.title: What Building a Tournament Bracket Engine Taught Me About Edge Cases
articles.description: When I started building Rollare, a free bracket maker for local sports clubs, I thought the hard part...
articles.body_html:
When I started building Rollare, a free bracket maker for local sports clubs, I thought the hard part would be drawing a nice bracket on screen. It wasn't. The hard part turned out to be everything that happens around the bracket: seeding order, bye distribution, rematch avoidance, and the dozen edge cases that only show up when a real organizer with 44 teams and a deadline hits your software on a Saturday morning.

Here are the lessons that cost us the most iterations.

Single elimination: seeding is not sorting

The first naive version sorted teams by seed and paired them 1v2, 3v4, and so on. Any bracket person will tell you that's wrong — it produces a final between seed 1 and seed 2 in the semifinal, not the final. Standard tournament seeding pairs 1 vs the last seed in the first round, which is why a 8-bracket looks like 1v8, 4v5, 3v6, 2v7: the structure exists so that top seeds can only meet as late as possible.

Getting this right for arbitrary sizes means working in powers of two: for a 12-team bracket you pad to 16, mark the missing slots as byes, and — this is the part people get wrong — byes must go to the highest seeds, never randomly. We ship a dedicated bye calculator because "how many byes and where" is genuinely the most-asked question organizers have.

Round robin: the circle method works until it doesn't

Scheduling a round robin is a solved problem — the circle method rotates all teams but one around a fixed pivot. But the edge cases bite:

  • Odd team counts need a ghost team, and every ghost match quietly becomes a bye. If you forget to filter ghosts from standings, a "Ghost" row wins the league.
  • Double round robin (home and away) is not "run the algorithm twice" — you have to reverse home/away in the second half, or every team plays two consecutive home games and venues complain.
  • Duplicate fixtures are the classic bug: if your round generation isn't deterministic per group, a 6-team group can end up with the same matchup twice in one half. We hit this with a real 44-team pickleball event split into 8 groups — deduplication had to happen at the group level, not the tournament level.

Swiss: pairing is a constraint problem wearing a smile

Swiss looks friendlier than elimination and is secretly the hardest. The rules everyone expects:

  1. Pair similar records (score buckets).
  2. Never rematch — players remember, and they will email you.
  3. Nobody gets two byes.
  4. Odd team out comes from the bottom bucket, not the top.

Rule 2 combined with rule 1 creates a graph matching problem. In small fields you can backtrack; in a 64-team esports qualifier you need a deterministic strategy or you'll time out on a phone. Our approach: sort within buckets, walk the bucket pairing the top remaining with the bottom remaining who isn't a rematch, and only then escalate to crossing buckets. Deterministic beats optimal — organizers care that the result is explainable.

Double elimination: the bracket reset

The grand finals of a double elimination bracket is weird by design: if the winners-bracket finalist loses — their first loss — the tournament isn't over, because both teams now have one loss. You run a bracket reset. If you model your tournament as a linear pipeline instead of a state machine, this "rematch everyone thought was the final" will break your results page, your standings, and your notifications all at once. Match status has to live on the match, not on the tournament.

Tiebreakers: the cycle nobody warns you about

Head-to-head first, then score differential, seems obvious. Then three teams finish in a cycle: A beat B, B beat C, C beat A. Head-to-head is undefined — you need a documented fallback order (differential, then points scored, then a coin-flip procedure) before the tournament starts. We ended up making tiebreak priority configurable per tournament, because a chess club and a volleyball league will argue forever about which metric comes first.

The export nobody asked for until they all asked

Organizers don't want a PDF of a database table; they want a poster they can print and stick on a clubhouse wall or drop into a WhatsApp group. We generate bracket posters as SVG and rasterize them server-side with resvg. Running a rasterizer on an edge runtime is its own adventure — the wasm runtime can't load anything at require-time, so fonts and binaries have to be static bindings baked into the build. That one constraint reshaped half of our build pipeline.

What real events changed

The biggest lesson had nothing to do with algorithms. Real organizers register teams on phones, in a rush, often all within an hour of a deadline (our current record: 19 signups in 32 minutes for a 64-team PES tournament shared in a WhatsApp group). Every flow that assumed "a person calmly fills this in at a desk" lost. If you're building anything event-shaped: registration, the bracket, and live score updates are one product, not three.

If you want to see these decisions in the wild — eight formats from single elimination to swiss, registration, scheduling, and printable results — everything is free at Rollare, and the tournament templates are a decent shortcut if you're running a standard club event.

articles.title: How to Build Your Team's First Shared Agent
articles.description: Most teams already use AI. The problem is that everyone uses it alone.  One developer has a prompt...
articles.body_html:
Most teams already use AI. The problem is that everyone uses it alone.

One developer has a prompt that writes great release notes. Someone in support has a chat thread that drafts perfect replies. A PM keeps a document of instructions they paste into a chatbot every Monday. None of it is shared, none of it is consistent, and when that person goes on leave, the workflow goes with them.

A shared agent fixes that. Instead of ten private assistants, the team gets one agent with the same instructions, the same data, and the same rules, available to everyone who needs it.

In this guide, I'll walk through how to build your team's first one: how to pick the right job, set it up safely, choose a platform, and roll it out without it turning into another tool nobody uses.

Personal Agent vs Shared Agent

A shared agent is not just a personal assistant with more users. Once a whole team depends on it, the design questions change.

Personal agent Shared agent
Who uses it One person A team, channel, or department
Instructions Lives in one person's head or chat history Written down, versioned, owned
Data access Whatever that person can see Scoped to what the whole team should see
Output quality Judged by one user Has to be consistent for everyone
When it breaks One person notices The whole workflow stalls
Owner The user A named person responsible for upkeep

The last row matters most. A shared agent without an owner slowly drifts out of date until people stop trusting it.

Step-by-Step: Building Your First Shared Agent

1. Pick one repetitive job, not a vision

The biggest mistake is starting with "an AI assistant for the whole team." That's too vague to build and too vague to judge.

Start with one job that already happens every week and follows a pattern. Good first candidates:

  • Standup or weekly summaries from tickets, commits, or channel activity
  • Triage of incoming bugs or support requests into the right queue
  • First drafts of release notes, changelogs, or customer replies
  • Internal Q&A over your docs, runbooks, and onboarding material

A simple test: if you can't describe the job in one sentence, it's too big for a first agent.

2. Write down what "good" looks like

Before touching any tool, collect three to five real examples of the output you want. Paste in last week's best release notes or the triage decisions a senior engineer made.

These examples become your instructions and, later, your test cases. Without them, every teammate judges the agent against a different picture in their head.

3. Decide where the agent lives

Put the agent where the team already talks. If your team works in Slack, a web app nobody opens will die quietly. If work lives in Jira or Teams, start there.

This single decision usually narrows your platform options to two or three. I cover those in the next section.

4. Connect only the data it needs

A shared agent sees what you give it, and everyone who uses it can potentially surface that data. So scope carefully:

  • Connect the specific channels, projects, or folders the job needs
  • Avoid private channels, HR folders, and anything with credentials
  • Prefer read-only access until the agent has earned trust

When in doubt, start narrower. Adding a source later is easy. Explaining why the agent quoted someone's salary is not.

5. Write instructions like an onboarding doc

Treat the agent's instructions the way you'd brief a new hire:

  • Role: what it's for and who it serves
  • Inputs: which sources to use, and which to ignore
  • Output format: structure, length, tone, with an example
  • Boundaries: what it should never do, and when to hand off to a human

Keep the instructions in a shared, versioned place, not inside one person's account.

6. Set permissions and an owner

Decide three things explicitly:

  1. Who can use it (a channel, a group, the whole org)
  2. Who can edit it (usually one or two people)
  3. Who owns it (one named person who reviews it monthly)

Most platforms separate "can use" from "can edit." Use that. A shared agent that anyone can quietly rewrite becomes unpredictable fast.

7. Pilot with a small group

Roll it out to three to five people for two weeks. Ask them to flag every bad answer, not just the dramatic ones. Feed those back into the instructions.

8. Measure something simple

You don't need a dashboard. Track one or two things:

  • How often people actually use it each week
  • How much of its output gets used with light edits versus rewritten

If usage drops after the first week, the agent isn't saving time yet. Fix that before expanding.

Where to Build It

You don't need to write an agent from scratch for your first one. Most teams already pay for a tool that can host a shared agent, and engineering teams have a dedicated option too. Pick based on where your team works, not on which model is trendiest.

If your team lives in Option How sharing works
Slack Claude Tag (Claude Team and Enterprise, in beta) One agent per channel that anyone there can @-mention; admins control which tools, data, and channels it can access
Microsoft Teams / M365 Copilot Studio Publish the agent to Teams, then share it with teammates or submit it to your org catalog
Jira / Confluence Atlassian Rovo agents (paid Cloud plans) Agents built in Rovo Studio run on your team's Jira and Confluence data, metered by Rovo credits
Google Workspace Gemini Gems Shared like a Google Drive file; recipients can use, edit, or copy the Gem
ChatGPT Business / Enterprise Custom GPTs Share invite-only, by link, or with the whole workspace, with "can chat," "can view settings," or "can edit" permissions

A few notes from comparing these:

  • Chat-native agents (Slack, Teams) get adopted fastest because nobody has to open a new tab.
  • Gems and custom GPTs are the quickest to set up, but they work best for reusable instructions plus documents, not for agents that act across your tools.
  • Rovo and Copilot Studio go deeper into their own ecosystems, which is great if your work already lives there and limiting if it doesn't.

Sharkly: for engineering teams sharing coding agents

If your team's first shared agent is a coding agent, the platforms above only solve part of the problem. Tools like Claude Code and Codex are powerful, but they usually run on one developer's machine, in one person's session. The rest of the team can't see what the agent is working on, who assigned it, or whether anyone reviewed the result.

That's the gap Sharkly is built for. It's a shared workspace where people and AI coding agents work from the same task board.

In practice, that means a team can:

  • Assign tasks to coding agents the same way they assign them to teammates
  • Run several agents in parallel, each in its own isolated worktree
  • Keep context, progress, and results together in one shared workflow
  • Add human review before agent work is accepted
  • Connect Jira, so agent runs stay traceable in existing project workflows

This maps neatly onto the steps in this guide. The task board gives the agent a clear job, the workspace makes ownership visible, and the review step keeps a human in the loop.

One distinction matters: Sharkly doesn't replace your coding agent. It adds the team layer of assignment, coordination, and review on top of tools your developers already use. According to Sharkly's own guide, it's free for organizations of up to 5 people, and agents don't take up seats.

For a small engineering team, that makes it an easy way to run a first shared-agent pilot without a budget conversation.

If none of these fit, frameworks and agent SDKs let you build your own. For a first agent, though, the platform you already pay for is almost always the right call.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Starting too broad. "Help the team with anything" produces an agent that's mediocre at everything. One job first.
  • Connecting everything. More data is not better data. Irrelevant sources make answers noisier and raise the risk of leaking something sensitive.
  • No owner. Instructions go stale, sources move, and nobody notices until the answers are wrong.
  • Letting everyone edit. Separate who uses the agent from who changes it.
  • Skipping the human check. For anything customer-facing or irreversible, the agent drafts and a person approves.
  • Measuring nothing. If you can't say whether it saves time, you can't justify expanding it.

Final Thoughts

Your first shared agent doesn't need to be impressive. It needs to be useful, trusted, and owned.

Pick one job your team repeats every week. Write down what good looks like. Put the agent where people already work, give it only the data it needs, and assign someone to keep it healthy.

Get that right once, and the second and third agents become much easier, because your team will already know how to brief, test, and trust them.

One job. One owner. One place. That's how teams move from personal AI to shared AI.

articles.title: The Fibonacci Spiral Is Secretly a Straight Line
articles.description: I folded it, unfolded it, and watched it flip to the other side. A three.js experiment, the math...
articles.body_html:
I folded it, unfolded it, and watched it flip to the other side. A three.js experiment, the math behind it, and a few myths worth busting.

You have seen the picture a thousand times: squares of size 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 snapped together like a puzzle, with a smooth spiral curling through them.

But here's a question worth asking: what happens if you unfold it?

I hinged every square to its neighbor, pressed play, and watched the spiral untwist. The squares swung open one after another, the curve loosened, and at the end it lay perfectly flat: one straight line running through every square.

No trick. No cheating. It falls straight out of the geometry. By the end of this post, you'll know this chain of arcs can be transformed into a straight line, how to animate the fold in three.js, and which Fibonacci facts are myths.

Credit where it is due: the idea came from a much bigger animation I saw on X (link to the original post here). This is my own take on one piece of it, built from scratch in three.js.

The spiral is a chain of quarter-circles

The classic Fibonacci spiral is not one curve. It is a chain of quarter-circle arcs, one per square. Each arc has a radius equal to the side of its square, so the arcs get bigger exactly as fast as the Fibonacci numbers do.

Here is the detail that makes the whole trick work:

A quarter-circle arc inside a square connects two opposite corners of that square.

It is centered on a third, adjacent corner and sweeps across to the corner on the far side. So the straight-line shortcut between the arc's two ends, its chord, is the square's diagonal, with lengths * sqrt(2).

So what we have is a train of squares where each one has a diagonal "track" attached, and the end of one track is the start of the next.

Now imagine rotating each square around the shared point where its track meets the next. If you rotate them until every diagonal points in the same direction, the tracks line up end to end.

There is one important detail, though: rotating the squares alone does not straighten the circular arcs. The arcs must also be deformed into their chords. That is what the animation does.
The spiral is a straight line that has been folded.

A free prediction

The unfolded line has a length we can compute before running any code. Each square contributes its diagonal, so:

length = sqrt(2) * (F1 + F2 + ... + Fn)

And there is a classic identity: the sum of the first n Fibonacci numbers is F(n+2) - 1.

With 9 squares, the sizes are 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34. They add up to 88, and F11 = 89, so 89 - 1 = 88. The straight line is exactly 88 * sqrt(2) units long, which you can read off from one Fibonacci number.

That's approximately 124.45 units.

This is a useful prediction because it comes entirely from the geometry. We can calculate the expected length before the animation runs, then check the result against the construction.

The twist: it folds the other way

My first version unfolded to the right and then folded back to the right, retracing its own steps. The animation that inspired me did something better: it unfolded on one side and refolded on the other.

This costs almost nothing, thanks to one more property of the squares: a square is symmetric across its own diagonal, and the chord is exactly that diagonal. Mirror a square across its chord and you get the same square back.

The trick is to let the animation continue past the straight configuration. Once an arc has been straightened to its chord, it can continue through that line and emerge as its reflection on the other side.

So the mirror-image spiral needs no new geometry. Each square keeps rotating around its hinge, twice as far as it needed to reach the straight line, and its arc flips to the other side of the chord. With a fold value t:

  • t = 0: the spiral, curling one way
  • t = 1: the straight line
  • t = 2: the mirror-image spiral, curling the other way

The animation loops 0 → 1 → 2 → 1 → 0, and the straight line is the hinge the whole thing swings through. Watch the slider do that, and the whole thesis lands in three seconds: the spiral on the left, the line in the middle, its mirror image on the right, all the same geometry.

Building it in three.js

Three pieces do all the work.

1. Tile the squares

First, generate the Fibonacci sequence. Then place the squares one at a time, cycling through the directions right, up, left, and down. A bounding box tracks the occupied region and determines where each new square goes. Its size comes from the next Fibonacci term.


const f = [1, 1];

while (f.length < n) {
  f.push(f[f.length - 1] + f[f.length - 2]);
}

let b = { x0: 0, x1: 1, y0: 0, y1: 1 };

const dirs = ['R', 'U', 'L', 'D'];

for (let i = 1; i < n; i++) {
  const s = f[i];
  const d = i === 1 ? 'R' : dirs[(i - 1) % 4];

  // Place the square according to d,
  // then update the bounding box.
}

Each square also remembers its arc: a center corner and a start and end angle, 90 degrees apart.

2. Fold with forward kinematics

This is the part that feels like magic. Each square is a rigid body attached to the previous one at a hinge: the end of its arc. For each square, I compute how far it must turn so that its chord points along one common direction, and then I animate with a fold value t from 0 to 1.

The code below uses the same property names as the actual demo. The arrays P and v store the starting hinge and chord vector, while d stores the rotation needed to align that chord with the common direction.
