let px = items[0].P[0];
let py = items[0].P[1];

items.forEach((it, i) => {
  const D = t * it.d;
  const c = Math.cos(D);
  const s = Math.sin(D);

  it.g.rotation.y = D;
  it.g.position.set(px, i * 0.012, -py);

  // Move the next hinge to the end of this rotated chord.
  px += it.v[0] * c - it.v[1] * s;
  py += it.v[0] * s + it.v[1] * c;
});

Here, P is the starting hinge point and v is the chord of the square, the same diagonal we talked about above. d is the angle each square must turn to bring its chord parallel to the common direction. The squares never separate, because every square starts exactly where the previous chord ended.

This is forward kinematics: each square's new position depends on the transformation of the previous square. Instead of moving every square independently, we propagate the hinge position along the chain.

3. Straighten the curve itself

There is one catch. If the squares just rotate, the curve stays an arc inside each square. At t = 1 the chords line up, but the curve would still wobble through each diamond.

The fix is to blend each arc point toward the matching point on its chord as t goes up, then rebuild the tube geometry every frame:

const pts = arcPoints.map((p, j) =>
  p.clone().lerp(chordPoints[j], t)
);

mesh.geometry.dispose();

mesh.geometry = new THREE.TubeGeometry(
  new THREE.CatmullRomCurve3(pts),
  48,
  radius,
  6
);

At t = 0 you have the familiar spiral you came for. At t = 1 every arc lies along its chord, forming a straight line in the underlying 2D construction.

The implementation rebuilds the tube on every update. That's simple and works well for this small demo, although a larger, performance-sensitive scene could benefit from updating existing geometry instead.

Push t past 1 and the same formula overshoots: at t = 2 every point lands on the opposite side of its chord, so the arc is mirrored. That one line is the whole left-hand spiral.

One small implementation detail: the demo offsets successive square groups slightly in height to give the geometry some visual separation. If you remove that offset, the construction can lie in one plane, matching the ideal 2D geometry more closely.

Bonus: six ways to compute the numbers

The demo needs about a dozen terms, so a plain loop is plenty. If you want to explore much larger Fibonacci indices, the choice of algorithm starts to matter.

1. Naive recursion, O(φⁿ)

The version everyone writes first. It mirrors the definition perfectly and recomputes the same values again and again, so the running time grows exponentially. fib(40) is already noticeably slow.

const fib = n => (n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2));

2. Recursion with memoization, O(n)

Same recursion, but each result is remembered the first time it is computed, so every value is calculated once.

const memo = new Map();

function fib(n) {
  if (n < 2) return n;
  if (memo.has(n)) return memo.get(n);

  const value = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
  memo.set(n, value);
  return value;
}

3. The loop, O(n)

Add the previous two terms: f[i] = f[i-1] + f[i-2]. With JavaScript Number, all Fibonacci integers through F78 are exactly representable, but F79 exceeds the safe-integer limit. Past that, use BigInt if you need exact integer results.

4. A generator (lazy stream)

Instead of building an array of a fixed size, produce the numbers one at a time and take only as many as you need. With BigInt it stays exact forever.

function* fibs() {
  let [a, b] = [0n, 1n];
  while (true) {
    yield a;
    [a, b] = [b, a + b];
  }
}

const it = fibs();
const firstTen = Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => it.next().value);

5. Fast doubling, O(log n) recursive steps

Two identities let you jump from k to 2k directly: F(2k) = F(k) * (2F(k+1) - F(k)) and F(2k+1) = F(k)^2 + F(k+1)^2.

function fib(n) { // returns [F(n), F(n+1)]
  if (n === 0) return [0n, 1n];

  const [a, b] = fib(Math.floor(n / 2));
  const c = a * (2n * b - a);
  const d = a * a + b * b;

  return n % 2 === 1 ? [d, c + d] : [c, d];
}

6. Binet's formula: elegant, but numerically fragile

The expression φⁿ / √5 looks like a perfect shortcut: raise the golden ratio to the nth power, divide by √5, and round to the nearest integer. But a floating-point implementation can accumulate enough error to return the wrong integer. The mathematical formula is valid; the danger is evaluating it with finite-precision arithmetic. The exact point where it fails depends on the implementation and numeric precision.

The lesson: a closed-form formula is not automatically the best algorithm. Sometimes the elegant shortcut is less reliable than a simple loop.

Bonus bonus question: why can't floats just do it? φ is irrational, so a double can only store an approximation of it. Raising that approximation to the nth power multiplies the tiny error along with the value, so the absolute error grows as fast as φⁿ does. Once it passes 0.5, rounding lands on the wrong integer. The exact route is to avoid floats entirely and do the arithmetic with integers, which is essentially what fast doubling does.

Four Fibonacci myths worth busting

Since we are here, four things people get wrong about this picture:

  • It is not exactly the golden spiral. A true golden spiral grows by the factor phi (about 1.618) every quarter turn. The Fibonacci spiral only approximates that, because ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers get closer and closer to phi without ever hitting it. The quarter-circles also meet with matching tangents (G1 continuity), so there are no kinks. But the curvature jumps at every joint, because the radius changes abruptly from one square to the next. A true golden spiral has smoothly changing curvature.
  • The nautilus shell is not a golden spiral. Its overall shape can be approximated by a logarithmic spiral, but its growth rate is not guaranteed to match the golden ratio. The familiar golden-rectangle overlay is a mathematical illustration, not evidence that the shell follows that exact construction.
  • Fibonacci patterns in nature are real, but narrower than the memes suggest. The best example is plants. Sunflowers, pinecones, and pineapples often display spiral counts corresponding to consecutive Fibonacci numbers. In phyllotaxis models, these patterns are associated with growth at angles close to the golden angle, about 137.5 degrees. The biological mechanisms are more complex than a single mathematical rule, which makes the subject even more interesting.
  • "Fibonacci" was not his name. The man was Leonardo of Pisa. "Fibonacci" is generally explained as a contraction of filius Bonacci, "son of Bonacci", and the nickname seems to have caught on centuries after he died. He did not discover the sequence either: Indian mathematicians had described it long before, and Leonardo brought it to Europe in his 1202 book Liber Abaci.

Try it

The full demo is in the Pen above. Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, and use the Fold slider to scrub from the spiral (0) through the straight line (1) to its mirror image (2), and press H to hide the controls for a clean view.
Try changing the number of terms and watch the straight line get longer. Each added term adds exactly F(n) * sqrt(2) to its length.

Some ideas to take further:

  1. Label each square with its Fibonacci number.
  2. Color the squares by their ratio to the previous one and watch it settle toward phi.
  3. Build the sunflower version: place points at multiples of 137.5 degrees and see the spirals appear.

If you build something with this, I would love to see it. Share it in the comments.

articles.title: TypeScript Function Overloads in 2026: When They Clarify and When They Mislead the Caller
articles.description: Function overloads promise precise type inference, but first-match resolution and order dependency create maintainability traps. This guide shows when overloads clarify intent and when union types deliver better outcomes.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript Function Overloads in 2026: When They Clarify and When They Mislead the Caller

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Function overloads in TypeScript let developers declare multiple signatures for a single function, each promising a different relationship between inputs and outputs. The feature sounds clean on paper: one function name, multiple valid call patterns, all type-checked. The TypeScript compiler resolves which signature matches at each call site, and developers get precise return types without runtime branching.

The problem surfaces when teams write overloads without understanding the first-match resolution rule documented in the TypeScript handbook. The compiler tests signatures in declaration order and stops at the first compatible match. A later, more specific signature never runs if an earlier, broader one already fits the arguments. The code compiles, callers see the wrong return type, and the confusion spreads through a codebase. Teams add more overloads to fix edge cases, the signature list grows to six or eight entries, and nobody can predict which one will match a given call.

Function overload problem — compiler picks wrong signature

The solution is to recognize when overloads add value and when they obscure intent. Overloads clarify APIs when different argument shapes truly require different return types, a pattern common in DOM APIs and framework entry points. Union types serve better when the function logic treats all inputs uniformly. Understanding resolution order, maintaining signature consistency, and choosing the simpler tool when both work keeps overload sets readable.

Function overload solution — correct signature selection

Key Takeaways

  • TypeScript resolves overload signatures using first-match logic in declaration order, not by choosing the most specific match.
  • Overloads clarify APIs when different argument shapes require different return types; union types serve better for uniform handling.
  • Signature order determines which overload the compiler selects, making consistency and narrow-to-broad ordering critical.
  • Overload sets exceeding three signatures often signal that a discriminated union or generic constraint would communicate intent more clearly.
  • The implementation signature must accept all overload cases but remains invisible to callers, creating a maintenance gap when signatures diverge.

How TypeScript Resolves Overload Signatures: First Match Wins

The compiler tests overload signatures in the order developers write them, stopping at the first compatible match. When a function call passes type checking against an overload signature, TypeScript uses that signature's return type and never evaluates later entries. This resolution rule appears in the type compatibility section of the official handbook: "When a function has overloads, each overload in the target type must be matched by a compatible signature on the source type."

function parse(input: string): string;
function parse(input: number): number;
function parse(input: string | number): string | number {
  return typeof input === 'string' ? input.toUpperCase() : input * 2;
}

const result1 = parse('hello'); // type: string
const result2 = parse(42); // type: number

The example above works because the compiler checks parse('hello') against the first signature, finds a match, and assigns the return type string. The second call checks against the second signature first (the string signature does not match a number argument), matches, and returns number. Both callers see precise types.

The failure mode appears when an earlier signature accepts the same arguments as a later one. The compiler matches the broader signature first and never reaches the specific case.

function process(data: string | number): string | number;
function process(data: string): string;
function process(data: string | number): string | number {
  return typeof data === 'string' ? data.toUpperCase() : data * 2;
}

const result = process('test'); // type: string | number (not string)

TypeScript function overload resolution order

The caller passes a string, which satisfies both signatures. The compiler tests the first signature (string | number parameter), matches, and uses its return type (string | number). The second signature never runs. The developer intended process('test') to return string, but the signature order prevents that inference.

The solution places narrow signatures before broad ones. The compiler stops at the first match, so developers must write the most specific cases first.

function process(data: string): string;
function process(data: number): number;
function process(data: string | number): string | number {
  return typeof data === 'string' ? data.toUpperCase() : data * 2;
}

const result = process('test'); // type: string

Reordering the signatures lets the compiler test the string case first, match it, and return the specific type. The union signature sits last as a fallback. The implementation signature at the end must still accept all parameter combinations because the runtime executes only one function body.

When Overloads Clarify Intent: DOM APIs and Multiple Signatures

Overloads improve clarity when a function accepts fundamentally different argument shapes that map to distinct return types. The DOM querySelector method demonstrates this pattern: calling it with a tag name returns a specific element type, while a generic selector returns a more general Element.

function querySelector(selectors: 'div'): HTMLDivElement | null;
function querySelector(selectors: 'span'): HTMLSpanElement | null;
function querySelector(selectors: string): Element | null;
function querySelector(selectors: string): Element | null {
  return document.querySelector(selectors);
}

const div = querySelector('div'); // type: HTMLDivElement | null
const span = querySelector('span'); // type: HTMLSpanElement | null
const generic = querySelector('.class'); // type: Element | null

The function signature communicates three guarantees without conditional types or runtime checks. Callers passing 'div' receive a narrower type than callers using a class selector. The TypeScript compiler enforces this relationship because the first two signatures handle specific string literals, and the third signature catches all other string inputs.

Framework entry points often follow this pattern. A routing library might return different handler types based on the HTTP method.

function route(method: 'GET', path: string): GetHandler;
function route(method: 'POST', path: string): PostHandler;
function route(method: 'PUT', path: string): PutHandler;
function route(method: string, path: string): Handler {
  // implementation
}

Each signature maps a specific method string to its corresponding handler type. Callers see distinct return types without inspecting the implementation. The overload list serves as documentation, showing which methods the function supports.

The value disappears when signatures differ only in optional parameters or when the return type stays constant across all cases. Overloads add noise without improving type inference.

// No benefit — union type works better
function log(message: string, level: 'info'): void;
function log(message: string, level: 'warn'): void;
function log(message: string, level: 'error'): void;
function log(message: string, level: string): void {
  console.log(`[${level}] ${message}`);
}

// Simpler with union
function log(message: string, level: 'info' | 'warn' | 'error'): void {
  console.log(`[${level}] ${message}`);
}

The overload version requires four signature declarations to express what a union type handles in one line. The return type stays void in every case, so the extra signatures provide no inference benefit. Developers reading the code must parse multiple lines to understand a simple constraint.

When Overloads Mislead: Order Matters and Hidden Complexity

Overload order creates a maintenance trap when teams add new signatures without auditing existing ones. A function starts with two overloads, a third case appears months later, and the developer appends it at the end. The compiler matches an earlier signature first, and the new case never runs.

Consider a validation function that evolved over several iterations:

// Original design
function validate(input: string): boolean;
function validate(input: number): boolean;
function validate(input: string | number): boolean {
  return input.toString().length > 0;
}

// Later addition (appended at end)
function validate(input: string): boolean;
function validate(input: number): boolean;
function validate(input: { value: string }): string; // New case
function validate(input: string | number | { value: string }): boolean | string {
  if (typeof input === 'object') return input.value;
  return input.toString().length > 0;
}

The third signature never matches because the compiler stops at the first string or number overload. Callers passing { value: 'test' } see a type error because no signature accepts that shape at the top of the list. The developer must reorder signatures to fix the issue, but the codebase may already rely on the existing order for other call sites.

Signature ordering Compiler behavior Caller experience
Narrow types first Matches specific cases early, fallback types last Precise inference, predictable resolution
Broad types first Matches general cases early, specific types unreachable Imprecise inference, silent fallback
Inconsistent order Matches depend on declaration sequence Unpredictable inference, maintenance burden

Overload resolution comparison — narrow vs broad first

The implementation signature compounds the problem. It must accept all parameter combinations from every overload, but callers never see it. Developers change an overload without updating the implementation signature, and the function compiles but crashes at runtime when an edge case hits the unhandled path.

function transform(input: string): string;
function transform(input: number): number;
function transform(input: string | number): string | number {
  // Forgot to handle number case
  return input.toUpperCase(); // Runtime error if input is number
}

The implementation signature promises to accept string | number, but the body only handles strings. TypeScript permits this gap because the implementation signature remains invisible to external callers. The function compiles, runtime tests pass if they only cover string inputs, and the production crash happens when a number arrives.

Overloads vs Union Types: Choosing the Right Tool in 2026

Union types handle cases where the function treats all inputs uniformly. Overloads serve cases where different inputs require different return types. The decision tree appears simple, but teams often default to overloads when union types would deliver clearer intent.

A formatting function demonstrates the distinction:

// Overloads (unnecessary complexity)
function format(value: string, style: 'uppercase'): string;
function format(value: string, style: 'lowercase'): string;
function format(value: string, style: 'capitalize'): string;
function format(value: string, style: string): string {
  switch (style) {
    case 'uppercase': return value.toUpperCase();
    case 'lowercase': return value.toLowerCase();
    case 'capitalize': return value.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + value.slice(1);
    default: return value;
  }
}

// Union type (clearer)
function format(
  value: string,
  style: 'uppercase' | 'lowercase' | 'capitalize'
): string {
  switch (style) {
    case 'uppercase': return value.toUpperCase();
    case 'lowercase': return value.toLowerCase();
    case 'capitalize': return value.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + value.slice(1);
  }
}

The overload version requires four signatures to constrain a single parameter. The return type stays string in every case, so the extra declarations add no type-safety benefit. The union version communicates the same constraint in one signature. Callers see the same autocomplete options, the same type errors for invalid styles, and the implementation stays identical.

TypeScript overloads versus union types decision tree

Overloads add value when the return type changes based on argument shape. A data fetcher that returns different response structures based on the endpoint demonstrates appropriate overload use:

function fetch(endpoint: '/users'): Promise<User[]>;
function fetch(endpoint: '/posts'): Promise<Post[]>;
function fetch(endpoint: '/comments'): Promise<Comment[]>;
function fetch(endpoint: string): Promise<unknown> {
  return globalThis.fetch(endpoint).then(r => r.json());
}

const users = await fetch('/users'); // type: User[]
const posts = await fetch('/posts'); // type: Post[]

Each endpoint returns a distinct type. A union type cannot express this relationship without conditional types or discriminated unions, both of which push complexity into the type system. Overloads keep the signature list flat and readable.

Scenario Union types Overloads Recommended approach
Same return type, constrained parameter Single signature, clear constraint Multiple signatures, repeated return type Union types
Different return types per argument Requires conditional types or generics Natural signature mapping Overloads
Optional parameters only Single signature with optional markers Multiple signatures with incremental parameters Union types
Runtime behavior varies by type Union parameter, type guards in body Overload signature, type narrowing at call site Depends on call-site complexity

Overload vs union type decision flow

The choice impacts maintainability. Overload sets grow as new cases appear, while union types extend by adding another member to the union. A function with six overloads becomes harder to audit than a union with six members because developers must verify signature order and consistency across all entries.

Production Patterns: Writing Maintainable Overload Sets

Maintainable overload sets follow three rules: narrow signatures precede broad ones, the implementation signature accepts all cases, and the total signature count stays below four. When a function exceeds four overloads, the signature list obscures intent more than it clarifies.

The signature ordering rule addresses first-match resolution. The compiler stops at the first compatible signature, so the most specific cases must appear first.

// Correct ordering
function process(input: 'start'): StartResult;
function process(input: 'stop'): StopResult;
function process(input: string): GeneralResult;
function process(input: string): StartResult | StopResult | GeneralResult {
  if (input === 'start') return { type: 'start', timestamp: Date.now() };
  if (input === 'stop') return { type: 'stop', timestamp: Date.now() };
  return { type: 'general', value: input };
}

String literal types appear before the string union. The compiler checks 'start' and 'stop' before falling back to the general case. Callers passing specific literals see narrow return types. Callers passing other strings see the general type.

Overload signature resolution with narrow-to-broad ordering

The implementation signature must handle all parameter combinations from every overload. Mismatches between overload signatures and the implementation create runtime gaps.

// Dangerous — implementation does not cover all overloads
function transform(input: string): string;
function transform(input: number): number;
function transform(input: boolean): boolean; // Added later
function transform(input: string | number): string | number {
  // Missing boolean case
  if (typeof input === 'string') return input.toUpperCase();
  return input * 2;
}

The third overload promises to accept boolean inputs, but the implementation signature excludes them. TypeScript permits this because the implementation signature stays internal. The function compiles, and the boolean case crashes at runtime. Teams prevent this gap by ensuring the implementation signature always union-matches all overload parameters.

Signature count matters. Three overloads communicate distinct cases without overwhelming readers. Six overloads demand a refactor into discriminated unions or mapped types.

// Too many overloads (hard to maintain)
function request(method: 'GET', url: string): Promise<string>;
function request(method: 'POST', url: string, body: string): Promise<string>;
function request(method: 'PUT', url: string, body: string): Promise<string>;
function request(method: 'DELETE', url: string): Promise<string>;
function request(method: 'PATCH', url: string, body: string): Promise<string>;
function request(method: 'HEAD', url: string): Promise<void>;
function request(method: string, url: string, body?: string): Promise<string | void> {
  // implementation
}

// Better with discriminated union
type RequestConfig =
  | { method: 'GET' | 'DELETE' | 'HEAD'; url: string }
  | { method: 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'PATCH'; url: string; body: string };

function request(config: RequestConfig): Promise<string | void> {
  // implementation
}

The discriminated union collapses six signatures into two union members. Callers construct objects instead of passing positional arguments, but the type system enforces the same constraints. The function signature stays flat, and adding new methods requires extending the union instead of appending another overload.

Common Mistakes: Inconsistent Return Types and Unreachable Signatures

Return type inconsistency appears when developers add overloads without coordinating the implementation. The overload signatures promise one type, the implementation returns another, and TypeScript accepts the mismatch because the implementation signature remains invisible.

function parse(input: string): number;
function parse(input: number): string;
function parse(input: string | number): string | number {
  // Implementation returns wrong type for string input
  if (typeof input === 'string') return input; // Should return number
  return input.toString(); // Should return string
}

const result1 = parse('123'); // type: number, runtime: string
const result2 = parse(123); // type: string, runtime: string

The first overload promises string input returns number, but the implementation returns the string unchanged. TypeScript infers the return type as number based on the overload signature, but the runtime value stays a string. Operations expecting a number crash when the string arrives. The noImplicitReturns compiler option catches missing return statements but not type mismatches between overload promises and implementation behavior.

Unreachable signatures appear when a broad signature precedes a narrow one. The compiler matches the broad case first and never evaluates later entries.

// Second signature unreachable
function handle(input: unknown): string;
function handle(input: string): string; // Never matches
function handle(input: unknown): string {
  return typeof input === 'string' ? input : String(input);
}

const result = handle('test'); // Uses first signature (unknown parameter)

The first signature accepts unknown, which matches any argument including string. The compiler stops there and never checks the second signature. Callers passing strings see the first signature's return type, which happens to match the second signature in this example but obscures the intended narrow match. Linters do not flag unreachable signatures because the function remains type-safe, the issue surfaces as unexpected inference behavior rather than a compile error.

The fix reorders signatures or removes redundant ones. When signatures overlap, the narrow case must appear first. When signatures provide no additional inference benefit, removing them clarifies intent.

// Corrected ordering
function handle(input: string): string;
function handle(input: unknown): string;
function handle(input: unknown): string {
  return typeof input === 'string' ? input : String(input);
}

const result = handle('test'); // Uses first signature (string parameter)

Redundant overloads appear when developers add signatures that provide no additional type information. A function with three overloads that differ only in parameter names wastes declaration space.

// Redundant overloads
function calculate(a: number, b: number): number;
function calculate(x: number, y: number): number;
function calculate(first: number, second: number): number;
function calculate(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a + b;
}

Parameter names do not affect type checking. All three signatures accept two numbers and return a number. The extra declarations add no value. A single signature communicates the same constraint.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should a function use overloads instead of union types?

Use overloads when different argument shapes map to different return types and the function cannot express that relationship through a single union type. DOM APIs like querySelector demonstrate this pattern: passing a specific tag name returns a narrow element type, while a generic selector returns Element. Union types serve better when the return type stays constant across all argument combinations or when the function handles all inputs uniformly. Overload sets exceeding three signatures usually signal that a discriminated union or conditional type would communicate the design more clearly.

Does TypeScript choose the most specific overload signature or the first match?

TypeScript uses first-match resolution as documented in the type compatibility handbook. The compiler tests overload signatures in declaration order and stops at the first compatible match. A more specific signature later in the list never runs if an earlier, broader signature already accepts the arguments. This behavior requires developers to order signatures from narrow to broad, placing specific cases before general fallbacks. Signature ordering determines which return type callers see, making declaration sequence a critical part of overload design.

Why does the implementation signature stay invisible to callers?

The implementation signature defines the function body's parameter and return types but does not participate in call-site type checking. TypeScript uses only the overload signatures to infer types at call sites. This separation lets developers write a general implementation that handles all cases while exposing specific signatures to callers. The gap creates a maintenance risk: overload signatures can promise types the implementation does not deliver, and TypeScript accepts the mismatch because the implementation signature remains internal. Teams address this by ensuring the implementation signature accepts a union of all overload parameters and returns a union of all overload return types.

Can overload signatures have different parameter counts?

Yes, overload signatures can vary parameter counts to model functions with optional behavior based on argument presence. The implementation signature must accept all possible parameter combinations, typically by marking later parameters optional or using rest parameters. The compiler matches the first signature where all required parameters fit the call arguments. This pattern works for functions like event handlers where passing additional context arguments changes behavior, but it requires careful ordering to prevent broader signatures from shadowing narrower ones.

What compiler options affect overload behavior?

The strictBindCallApply option enables precise type checking for call, bind, and apply methods on overloaded functions, ensuring arguments match the selected signature. The noImplicitReturns option catches missing return statements in the implementation but does not verify that return types match overload promises. No compiler option currently warns about unreachable overload signatures or inconsistent return types between overloads and implementation. Teams rely on code review and testing to catch those gaps.

Conclusion

Function overloads in TypeScript clarify APIs when different argument shapes require different return types, but first-match resolution and order dependency create maintainability traps that grow with signature count. Narrow signatures must precede broad ones to prevent the compiler from stopping at an imprecise match. Union types deliver better outcomes when the return type stays constant or when the function handles all inputs uniformly. Keeping overload sets below four signatures, ensuring the implementation signature accepts all cases, and auditing signature order during code review prevent the confusion that emerges when developers add new cases without understanding resolution rules. Teams that recognize when overloads add value and when they obscure intent build APIs that communicate constraints through types rather than documentation.

HTTP vs HTTPS: What Really Happens When You Browse

In most browsers the difference between http:// and https:// looks like just a visual detail: a lock icon or a “not secure” warning. Beneath that appearance lie critical processes that determine whether the information you send and receive is protected or vulnerable. In this article we break down, in a practical and straightforward way, what happens at each step of the communication, what the real advantages of HTTPS are, and when (if ever) it still makes sense to use HTTP.

1. How HTTP Works: the Web’s Unprotected “Language”

HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) defines how browsers request resources (pages, images, scripts) and how servers deliver them. According to the Underc0de guide, “HTTP is the language your browser uses to ask for pages and the servers use to respond” [6].

The process is simple:

  1. Client → Server: The browser opens a TCP connection and sends a request (e.g., GET /index.html).
  2. Server → Client: The server replies with the requested resource and a status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found, etc.).

The entire exchange occurs in plain text. Any device that intercepts the connection (a router, an ISP, or an attacker on the same Wi‑Fi network) can read, copy, or modify the data without the user noticing. Therefore, HTTP provides no confidentiality or integrity guarantees.

2. HTTPS: HTTP Protected by TLS

HTTPS keeps the same request‑response structure but adds a security layer via TLS (Transport Layer Security). The NetworkTechnology guide explains that “HTTPS preserves that conversation, but protects it with TLS to provide encryption, integrity, and server authentication” [2].

Key steps are:

Step What Happens Why It Matters
TLS Handshake The client and server negotiate encryption algorithms and the server sends its digital certificate. The certificate verifies that the server is who it claims to be (authentication).
Encryption All requests and responses are encrypted with keys derived from the handshake. Prevents third parties from reading the content (confidentiality).
Integrity Each message includes a Message Authentication Code (MAC) that detects tampering. Stops an attacker from altering data in transit.

The result is a connection that, although it still uses HTTP to describe the request, exposes nothing in plain text. Browsers indicate this with the lock icon and, in some cases, with a “Secure” label. SiteGround notes that “HTTPS protects your data and the integrity of the information traveling between the client and the server” [5].

3. Concrete Benefits of Moving to HTTPS

3.1 Data Security

  • Confidentiality: Credentials, personal data, or payment information are encrypted.
  • Integrity: Content cannot be altered without the browser detecting it.
  • Authentication: The SSL/TLS certificate guarantees that the site you connect to is legitimate, reducing phishing risk.

3.2 SEO Impact and User Trust

Various guides indicate that search engines favor sites that use HTTPS, translating into better rankings [3]. Moreover, users trust sites that display the lock icon; its absence can generate distrust and abandonment.

3.3 Best Practices and Regulatory Compliance

The Programmer’s Blog highlights that, in 2026, most privacy standards (such as GDPR) require protection of data in transit, and HTTPS is the simplest way to meet that requirement [1]. Likewise, SiteGround’s guide recommends using HTTPS as the default configuration for any new web project.

4. When (If) HTTP Might Still Be Justified

Although HTTPS is the recommended choice almost universally, there are limited scenarios where HTTP can be acceptable:

  • Fully public, non‑interactive content: For example, a static page that only displays public information and does not collect user data.
  • Internal development environments: In closed networks where access control is guaranteed, some teams choose HTTP to simplify testing.

Keyfactor warns that “HTTPS still cannot hide the server’s IP address or connection metadata,” meaning that even though the content is encrypted, certain data remains visible [4]. For that reason, even in the scenarios above, it is wise to assess whether the reduction in complexity justifies the potential exposure of network‑level information.

5. Conclusion

HTTP and HTTPS share the same request‑response logic but differ dramatically in how they handle information in transit. While HTTP delivers data in plain text, HTTPS wraps it in a TLS layer that provides encryption, integrity, and authentication. The advantages of adopting HTTPS go beyond security: they improve SEO, increase user confidence, and simplify compliance with privacy regulations. Only in very specific situations (purely public content or controlled environments) might HTTP be considered, but even then the risks should be carefully evaluated.

6. Ready to Secure Your Site?

If you haven’t migrated your project to HTTPS yet, the next step is to obtain a TLS certificate (many Certificate Authorities offer them for free) and configure your server to redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS. Guides like Underc0de’s include detailed migration steps [6].

Don’t wait any longer! Implement HTTPS today and give your users the peace of mind that comes from browsing in a safe and trustworthy environment.

  • Diferencias entre HTTP y HTTPS | Guía Completa (Consultoría Informática)
  • HTTP frente a HTTPS: la verdadera diferencia | Keyfactor

articles.title: Crows, Moths, and Makefiles: How 300 Megabytes of Crow DNA Explains Why a 20-Kilobyte Scar File Outsmarts a Terabyte LLM
articles.description: Why do New Caledonian crows bend wire into hooks with zero training while a trillion-parameter LLM flies straight into the same production bug zapper? How Anthony Zador's Genomic Bottleneck explains what 'instinct' really is in AI coding agents.
articles.body_html:
Why can a New Caledonian crow bend a piece of wire into a hook on the first try—when no crow ancestor ever saw wire in nature—while a trillion-parameter LLM flies straight into the same 3 AM production bug zapper? Because evolution gave the crow a 20-kilobyte Makefile, and we gave the LLM a moth's porch light.

"Animals are born with highly structured brain connectivity, which enables them to learn very rapidly. Because the genome's capacity is orders of magnitude smaller than the number of synapses, the genome cannot specify the exact wiring diagram directly; instead, it specifies rules through a 'Genomic Bottleneck.'" — Anthony M. Zador, Nature Communications (2019)

"In the context of Scars, is there an equivalent of 'instinct' for an LLM? Would that be perhaps immutable parts of the training? Core knowledge? I was thinking about how crows seem to have amazing emergent problem-solving abilities, and how that must be instinct then, but how was that stored in the DNA?" — Randal L. Schwartz

1. The Betty the Crow Mystery: How Do You Store Wire-Bending in DNA?

If you have never watched the classic Oxford University footage of Betty, a New Caledonian crow (Corvus moneduloides), stop and picture the experiment (Weir, Chappell, & Kacelnik, 2002).

A small bucket of food is sitting at the bottom of a vertical glass tube. Next to the tube is a straight piece of laboratory garden wire—a human-manufactured metal alloy that zero generations of crows have ever encountered in 30 million years of evolution.

Betty picks up the straight wire, pokes it into the tube, realizes a straight shaft cannot lift the bucket handle, wedges the tip of the wire into a crevice in the tray base, pulls laterally with her beak to bend a 90-degree hook, and fishes the bucket out of the tube.

In another famous experiment (Jelbert et al., 2014), New Caledonian crows are presented with a narrow tube partially filled with water and a floating worm just out of reach—literally Aesop's Fable (The Crow and the Pitcher). Without training, the crows ignore floating Styrofoam blocks, select heavy sinking stones, and drop them one by one into the water until the displaced water level rises high enough to grab the worm.

Now ask the computer scientist's question:

How on Earth is that stored in the crow's DNA?!

Do the information-theory math—what neuroscientist Anthony Zador at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory famously called The Genomic Bottleneck (2019):

  • A New Caledonian crow's entire genome has roughly 1.2 billion base pairs (~300 MB of raw 2-bit data—less than a single CD-ROM, and only a tiny regulatory fraction of that 300 MB specifies brain wiring).
  • Yet the crow's brain (its avian pallium) contains over a billion neurons and trillions of synaptic weights.
  • Even more baffling: you cannot store "how to bend 20th-century steel garden wire" in DNA via Darwinian selection, because no ancestral crow ever touched steel wire!

So when we say the crow solved the puzzle by "instinct," what was actually in the DNA?

And more importantly for those of us building autonomous software engineering systems: what is the equivalent of "instinct" inside an LLM? Is it the frozen pre-trained weights? The core knowledge? Or have we been confusing two completely opposite biological instincts all along?

2. Two Kinds of Biological Instinct: The Moth vs. The Crow

When software engineers talk about an LLM's "instincts," they usually point to the immutable pre-trained weights (theta)—the hundreds of gigabytes of floating-point parameters frozen during pre-training and RLHF.

After all, when you type a prompt and the LLM immediately starts emitting Python or Dart code without consulting a manual, that looks like an instinct, right?

Yes—it is the exact instinct of a moth flying into a bug zapper.

In evolutionary biology, "instinct" is not one thing. Nature evolved two fundamentally different kinds of instinct, and comparing them reveals why unscarred LLMs fail in production:

flowchart TD
    subgraph Moth["🦋 Strategy A: The Moth's Instinct (Unscarred LLM Weights)"]
        M1["Hardwired Prior in Weights:\n'Keep brightest light at constant angle α'\n(In pre-training: 'Emit highest-frequency web tutorial')"]
        M2["In Ancestral Environment (The Moon at ∞):\nFlies in a straight line (Passes 10-line LeetCode demo)"]
        M3["In Production Environment (Porch Light at 2 meters):\nLogarithmic spiral straight into the bug zapper!\n(Vector 2: The Seductive 5-6-7-8 Trap)"]
        M1 --> M2 --> M3
    end

    subgraph Crow["🐦‍⬛ Strategy B: The Crow's Instinct (Synthetic Scars + Makefile DAG)"]
        C1["1. Innate Probing Loop in DNA (~20 KB WORKFLOW.mk):\n'Pick up stick → Poke crevice → Test physical leverage'\n(Target 15 Digraph → Target 30 TDD Red → Target 35 Green)"]
        C2["2. Spinal Nociception (Tier-1 Weights + 15ms AST Sensor):\n'If branch cracks or wire slips, recoil immediately'\n(15ms Linter + Target 40 Clean-Room Critic)"]
        C3["3. Flock Cultural Scolding (SCAR_REGISTRY.md):\n'One crow sees a trap → Whole flock learns in 12 seconds'\n(Target 90 4-Vector Scar Compilation)"]
        C1 --> C2 --> C3
    end

1. The Moth's Instinct: Hardwired Phototaxis (Vector 2: The Seductive 5-6-7-8)

Why do moths fly into flames and porch lights? Moths are not suicidal. For 100 million years before humans invented candles and LED bulbs, the only bright optical source at night was the Moon at optical infinity (d -> infinity).

If a flying insect wants to travel in a straight line at night, evolution can wire a dead-simple sensorimotor rule into its ganglia:

"Keep the brightest light source at a constant 30-degree angle to your compound eye."

When the light source is 384,400 kilometers away, keeping it at a constant 30-degree angle guarantees a perfectly straight flight path.

Now put that exact same moth in a backyard with a porch light two meters away (d << infinity). If you maintain a constant 30-degree angle to a point source at finite distance, basic geometry dictates that your flight path is a logarithmic spiral (r = a × e^(b × theta)) that terminates directly inside the flame.

An unscarred LLM's pre-trained weights (theta) are statistical phototaxis:

  • During pre-training on 10 trillion web tokens, the "Moon at infinity" is the Sunny-Day Tutorial Average (Page 1 of Google / Stack Overflow). In a 20-line stateless blog post, skipping StreamSubscription.cancel(), using wall-clock DateTime.now(), or firing unguarded parallel writes works fine.
  • When you drop that LLM into a stateful, concurrent production monorepo (the porch light at two meters), its immutable weight-instinct (argmax P(token | context)) follows the exact same constant-angle tutorial prior—and spirals straight into the 3 AM bug zapper!
  • In our 4-Vector Scar taxonomy, we call this Vector 2: The Trap (The Seductive 5-6-7-8). It feels like "core knowledge" to the model, just as the porch light looks like the Moon to the moth.

2. The Crow's Instinct: How 300 MB of DNA Bootstraps Emergent Genius

Now return to our New Caledonian crow. Why didn't Betty the Crow spiral into a loop when the straight wire failed to lift the bucket?

In 2005, Oxford biologists (Kenward et al., 2005) raised juvenile New Caledonian crows in controlled isolation where they never saw an adult crow use a tool. What happened? At a specific developmental week, every single young crow spontaneously began picking up twigs, poking them into holes, and prying against surfaces!

Wait—if DNA cannot store a lookup table of wire hooks, what did the crow's genome store?

Through Zador's Genomic Bottleneck, evolution compressed three tiny, universal primitives into the crow's DNA:

  1. An Innate Epistemic Probing Loop (The Scientific Method in Motor Circuits): The genome does not encode answers; it encodes an active probing sequence: > Grab object → Poke into boundary → Apply small test force → Observe physical resistance / displacement → Adjust geometry.
  2. Endogenous Nociception & Leverage Gradients (Pain + Sub-Goal Dopamine): The crow's brain is wired so that physical slippage or pain triggers an immediate motor halt (Circuit Breaker), while seeing the target move even 2 millimeters closer fires a striatal dopamine pulse.
  3. Rapid Amygdala Tagging & Cultural Flock Transmission (Cornell, Marzluff, & Pecoraro, 2011): In wildlife biologist John Marzluff's famous University of Washington experiments, researchers wore a specific caveman mask while trapping and banding just seven crows on campus, then released them unharmed.
    • Those crows immediately encoded a permanent somatic marker for that face.
    • Better yet: when a person walked across campus wearing that mask years later, huge mobs of crows—including young crows born years after the original trapping who had never been captured themselves—recognized the mask and dive-bombed the researcher with harsh scolding calls!
    • One crow touched the stove; the entire flock inherited the scar across generations.

3. The Biological-Mechanical Rosetta Stone: Mapping the Crow to Synthetic Scars

Look closely at the three pieces of the crow's intelligence, and you will see the exact architecture of Synthetic Scars (syntheticscars.org):

Biological Component in the Crow Information Size What Role It Plays Exact Equivalent in the Synthetic Scar Architecture
0. The Single Pyramidal Neuron (DNA's Cellular ALU) 1 Cell Blueprint (Replicated 10^9×) Dendritic dot product (w · x) + GABAergic divisive normalization (`
1. The Pallial Motor & Visual Cortex Billions of Synapses ({% raw %}Terabytes) Stores massive vocabulary of objects, shapes, and candidate muscle movements—but cannot tell a safe branch from a trap on its own. The LLM's Core Pre-Trained Weights (theta): Massive cosine-similarity engine (~1 TB) holding every programming language, SDK API, and design pattern—the motor cortex, NOT the survival instinct.
2. The Genomic Bottleneck (Innate Probing Loop) Tiny Regulatory DNA (Kilobytes) Hardwires the epistemic probing instinct: "Never leap blindly; poke the crevice with a stick first and feel how reality pushes back." WORKFLOW.mk / SKILL.md (~20 KB Declarative DAG): The immutable scientific-method loop—Target 15 (poke the strict digraph blast radius) → Target 30 (write a failing tdd-red test stick) → Target 35 (make it green).
3. Spinal Nociception & Pain Reflex Brainstem / Striatal Loop Instant recoil when a branch cracks or a tool slips (-∞ barrier). Tier-1 Scar-Aligned Weights (Rapid-Regret DPO) + 15ms AST Sensors + Target 40 Clean-Room Critic.
4. Flock Cultural Scolding Calls (Marzluff's Mask) Sparse Acoustic / Amygdala Signatures One crow gets trapped once; the warning signature spreads to every crow in the territory in seconds and persists for generations. SCAR_REGISTRY.md (The 4-Vector Scars): One agent collides at Target 90; within 12 seconds, the 4-Vector Scar (Wound, Trap, Circuit Breaker, Reflex) is committed to Git so no future agent ever touches that burner again (0.0% repeat regression rate across 256 tickets).

Wait—Even the Single Biological Neuron Is a DNA-Baked Cosine-Similarity Engine!

Stop and look at Row 0 of that table, because this is where the biological-mechanical overlap becomes almost spooky.

Earlier in this series (Part 4.1), I noted that all I really want a Google TPU to do is compute cosine similarity ("finding its cosine buddies") between the riverbanks of my Makefile.

Then I stopped and asked myself: Wait... how does DNA wire a biological neuron in the first place?!

Look at the biophysics of a single pyramidal neuron in a crow's pallium or your neocortex:

  1. Dendritic Dot Products + Divisive Normalization = Biological Cosine Similarity: A neuron has thousands of incoming dendritic synapses with weights w = [w_1, ..., w_n] receiving incoming spike firing rates x = [x_1, ..., x_n]. The cell body sums the weighted inputs (w · x), while local inhibitory interneurons (GABAergic basket cells; Carandini & Heeger, 2012) divide that signal by the total population activity ||x|| (divisive normalization—nature's exact LayerNorm + softmax!) and homeostatic synaptic scaling normalizes ||w||: 
   V_membrane  ~  (w · x) / (||w|| × ||x||)  =  cos(theta)

When the angle theta between the input vector x and the synaptic weight vector w approaches 0° (cos(theta) -> 1), the soma crosses -55 mV and fires an action potential!

  1. Embryonic Wiring via Molecular Q · K^T Barcodes (Sperry, 1963): How do growing axons find the right dendrites in the embryo before the crow even hatches? Under Roger Sperry's Nobel Prize–winning Chemoaffinity Hypothesis, DNA expresses combinatorial gradients of surface receptor proteins (ephrins, cadherins, protocadherins) on the growing axon tip (Query vector Q) and the target dendrite (Key vector K). When they touch, biochemical binding affinity is literally a molecular dot product (Q · K^T)!

Evolution didn't build a symbolic logic gate in DNA. DNA baked a self-normalizing cosine-similarity unit (the neuron), stamped out a billion copies of it to form a cortex, and then used a tiny 20-kilobyte Genomic Bottleneck script (WORKFLOW.mk) to wire those cosine engines into a stick-poking, pain-avoiding survival loop.

4. Why This Answers the "1,000-Scar Scaling" Question

Whenever engineers first see our Makefile workflow (WORKFLOW.mk) and our 618-scar registry, they often ask the exact same question biologists used to ask about crows:

"Wait a minute, Randal! An LLM has a terabyte of weights, and a production codebase has millions of possible bugs. How can a 20-kilobyte Makefile workflow and 5 phase-bound scars per step possibly keep a terabyte model from breaking things?!"

Now you know the answer—Zador's Genomic Bottleneck:

Biology's Genomic Bottleneck:
  |Crow Regulatory DNA| (~KBs)
